Others said: warn them that there is no god but Me, i.e., command them to monotheism together with frightening them if they do not affirm it.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 4:

Allah's saying: ﴿He created man from a drop of semen﴾. The commentators said: Ubayy ibn Khalaf took a decayed bone and began crumbling it, saying: "O Muhammad, how will Allah resurrect this after it has become dust?" So this verse was revealed concerning him. Al-khasim (the disputer) means the one who argues, and al-mubin (the open one) means the one whose contention is manifest.

The meaning: he was created from a drop of semen, yet despite this he argues and denies the resurrection. Should he not reason from his beginning to his end, and that the one who was able to bring him into existence at first is able to restore him a second time? In this there is also a reminder of Allah's favour upon him when He moved him from the weakness of the drop to the strength by which argument became possible for him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 5–7:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the cattle He created for you﴾. Al-an'am (cattle) are camels, cows, and sheep.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In them is warmth for you﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One: it is what is warmed by their wool, which is made into garments, tents, and other things. It was related by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "By warmth he means clothing." The majority of scholars went to this meaning.

The second: it is their offspring. It was related by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas: "﴿In them is warmth﴾, he said: al-difʾ (warmth) is the offspring of every animal." Ibn al-Sa'ib mentioned that he said: It is said that al-difʾ is their young, and those of the young that are not yet carrying. Ibn Faris the philologist related from al-Umawi who said: al-difʾ among the Arabs is the birth of camels and their milk.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And benefits﴾, i.e., apart from warmth: from their hides, their milk, their offspring, riding them, working with them, and other things. ﴿And from them you eat﴾, meaning: from the flesh of the cattle.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for you in them is beauty﴾, i.e., adornment, ﴿when you bring them back﴾, i.e., [when] you return them to their pen, which is the place where they shelter, and they come back with full udders and humps, and it is said: "This is the property of so-and-so." ﴿And when you send them out﴾, you release them in the morning to their pastures.

If it is asked: Why did He mention the returning (ruwah) first, when it comes second?

The answer: In the state of returning they are more beautiful, because they have grazed, their udders are full, and their humps are extended.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they carry your loads﴾. The reference by this is to what of them is able to bear loads. Al-athqal (loads) is the plural of thiql, which is the baggage of the traveller.

Concerning His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿to a land﴾, there are two opinions:

One: it is general, to every land the traveller intends. This is the saying of the majority.

The second: that what is meant by it is Makkah; this was said by 'Ikrimah. The first is more sound. The meaning is: they carry you to every land which, if you had undertaken to reach it yourselves, you would not have reached except with shiqq al-anfus (great hardship).

Concerning the meaning of "shiqq al-anfus" there are two opinions:

One: that it is hardship. This was said by the majority. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said: "We are in shiqq of life," i.e., in hardship; and in the hadith of Umm Zar': "﴿he found me among people of abundance in shiqq﴾."

The second: that shiqq means half, so hardship diminishes a man's strength and self as if half of him had gone; this was mentioned by al-Farra'.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾, i.e., when He bestowed upon you the blessings in which are these conveniences.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they carry your loads﴾. The reference by this is to what of them is able to bear loads. Al-athqal (loads) is the plural of thiql, which is the baggage of the traveller.

Concerning His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿to a land﴾, there are two opinions:

One: it is general, to every land the traveller intends. This is the saying of the majority.

The second: that what is meant by it is Makkah; this was said by 'Ikrimah. The first is more sound. The meaning is: they carry you to every land which, if you had undertaken to reach it yourselves, you would not have reached except with shiqq al-anfus (great hardship).

Concerning the meaning of "shiqq al-anfus" there are two opinions:

One: that it is hardship. This was said by the majority. Ibn Qutaybah said: It is said: "We are in shiqq of life," i.e., in hardship; and in the hadith of Umm Zar': "﴿he found me among people of abundance in shiqq﴾."

The second: that shiqq means half, so hardship diminishes a man's strength and self as if half of him had gone; this was mentioned by al-Farra'.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Most Kind, Most Merciful﴾, i.e., when He bestowed upon you the blessings in which are these conveniences.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 5–7:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the cattle He created for you﴾. Al-an'am (cattle) are camels, cows, and sheep.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿In them is warmth for you﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One: it is what is warmed by their wool, which is made into garments, tents, and other things. It was related by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "By warmth he means clothing." The majority of scholars went to this meaning.

The second: it is their offspring. It was related by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas: "﴿In them is warmth﴾, he said: al-difʾ (warmth) is the offspring of every animal." Ibn al-Sa'ib mentioned that he said: It is said that al-difʾ is their young, and those of the young that are not yet carrying. Ibn Faris the philologist related from al-Umawi who said: al-difʾ among the Arabs is the birth of camels and their milk.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And benefits﴾, i.e., apart from warmth: from their hides, their milk, their offspring, riding them, working with them, and other things. ﴿And from them you eat﴾, meaning: from the flesh of the cattle.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for you in them is beauty﴾, i.e., adornment, ﴿when you bring them back﴾, i.e., [when] you return them to their pen, which is the place where they shelter, and they come back with full udders and humps, and it is said: "This is the property of so-and-so." ﴿And when you send them out﴾, you release them in the morning to their pastures.

**Ibn al-Jawzi's commentary (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 16, verse 8:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the horses﴾, meaning: and He created the horses, ﴿and the mules and the donkeys, for you to ride and as adornment﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: and He created them as adornment.

Section

It is permissible to eat the flesh of horses. That it was not mentioned in the verse is because it is not the intended purpose; the main purpose of them is riding and adornment. This is the view of al-Shafi'i. Abu Hanifa and Malik said: the flesh of horses may not be eaten.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He creates what you do not know﴾. A group of the exegetes mentioned that what is meant by this is the wonders of creation in the heavens and the earth that have not been disclosed, such as what is related: that God has an angel of such-and-such a description, and beneath the Throne there is a river of such-and-such a description. Others said: it is what God has prepared in the Garden for its people, and in the Fire for its people. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said: some people disliked the explanation of this phrase. Al-Sha'bi said: this phrase is among the secrets of the Qur'an.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 9–11:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And upon Allah is the direction of the way﴾. Al-qasd (direction) means the straightness of the path. It is said: "a path qasd and qasid," when it leads you to what you intend. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: upon Allah is the clarifying of the straight path, and calling to it with proofs and evidence.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and of it is a deviating one﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: al-sabil (the way) is singular in form but is in the place of the plural, so it is as if He said: "and among the ways is a deviating way." Ibn al-Anbari said: When He mentioned al-sabil, it indicated al-subul (the ways), so He said ﴿and of it﴾, just as al-hadathan (the two changes of time) indicates al-hawadith (the calamities) in the words of al-Abdi:

"Nothing living remains against the changes of time, so will peace (al-salam) remain upon them?"

He meant: "so will it remain upon the calamities." Al-salam here means the rocks. He said: It is also possible that He said ﴿and of it﴾ because al-sabil is both feminine and masculine, so the meaning is: "of the way is a deviating one." Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning is: "and of the paths is one that is deviating, in which they do not find guidance." Al-ja'ir (the deviating) is the one who turns away from the direction (al-qasd). Ibn 'Abbas said: "and of them is the deviating one of the divergent desires." Ibn al-Mubarak said: "the desires and the innovations."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is He who sent down from the sky water﴾, meaning: the rain. ﴿For you from it is drink﴾, which is what you drink. ﴿And from it is a tree﴾. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two opinions regarding its meaning:

One: "and from it is the watering of trees and the drinking of trees," so the object of the preposition replaced the thing it governed, as in His saying: ﴿and they were made to drink the calf into their hearts﴾ [al-Baqara: 93].

The second: the meaning is "and from the direction of the water is a tree, and from its watering is a tree, and from its side is a tree," so the first was omitted and the second took its place. Zuhayr said:

"[To whom do these abodes belong at Qunnat al-Hijr...] ∗∗∗ they have been worn by the passage of years and months"

That is: "from the passage of years." Ibn Qutayba said: What is meant by this tree is pasture. Al-Zajjaj said: Everything that grows upon the earth is shajar (tree/plant). A poet, describing horses, said:

"He feeds them meat when shajar (vegetation) is scarce ∗∗∗ and feeding horses meat is harmful."

He means: they give the horses milk when the land is barren. And ﴿you pasture (tusimun)﴾ means: you graze (tar'un). It is said: "the camels pastured (sama), so they are grazing (sa'ima)" when they graze. It is taken from al-sawma, which is the mark, and its interpretation is that they leave marks upon the earth by their grazing.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He causes to grow for you thereby the crops﴾. Abu Bakr narrated from 'Asim: "nunbitu" with the nun. Ibn 'Abbas said: He means the grains. What follows this is clear, up to His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and the stars are subjected by His command﴾. Al-Akhfash said: The meaning is: "and He made the stars subjected," and it is permissible to supply a verb other than the first, because this supplied verb is in meaning like the expressed one, and the Arabs do even more than this. The rajiz (poet) said:

"You hear in their bellies a rumbling (sarad), and in the two hands dryness (jusa'a) and spreading (badad)."

The meaning is: "and you see in the two hands." Al-jus'a is dryness, and al-badad is breadth. Others said: His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿subjected﴾ is an emphatic circumstantial (hal), because their subjection has already been known from His saying, "and He subjected." Ibn 'Amir recited: "wal-shamsu wal-qamaru wal-nujumu musakharatun" with all of them in the nominative (raf'an), while Hafs narrated from 'Asim the accusative (nasb) as the majority recite, except His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and the stars are subjected﴾, for he made it nominative.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 12–16:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And what He has created for you﴾, meaning: and He subjected what He has created for you. Dhara'a (ذَرَأ) means: created. And "He subjected the sea" means: He made it submissive for riding and diving in it. "That you may eat from it fresh meat" means: fish. ﴿And that you may extract from it ornaments which you wear﴾ means: pearls, coral, and marjan (coral). (p-435) In this is evidence that if a person swore, "I will not wear ornaments," and then wore a pearl, he would break his oath. Abu Hanifa said: he would not break it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you see the ships﴾ means: the ships. Regarding the meaning of "mawakhir" (ploughing through), there are two views:

One: they are sailing, as said by Ibn Abbas. The linguists said: it is said "makhara al-safina makhran" when the ship cuts through the water in its course.

The second: "mawaqir" (laden), meaning filled, as said by al-Hasan.

Regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾ there are two views:

One: by riding in it for trade, seeking profit from the bounty of Allah.

The second: by what you extract from its ornaments and hunt from its fish. Ibn al-Anbari said: regarding the entry of the waw (و) in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾ there are two aspects:

One: that it is conjoined with a deleted lam, its estimation being: "And you see the ships ploughing in it, that you may benefit by that and that you may seek."

The second: that it has entered upon a hidden verb, its estimation being: "And He did that so that you may seek."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾ meaning: He set in it fixed mountains. ﴿Lest it should shake﴾ meaning: so that it would not shake. Al-Zajjaj said: "out of dislike that it should shake." It is said: "madda al-rajul yameed mayadan" when he is turned around with it. Ibn Qutayba said: al-mayd (ميد) is movement and inclination; it is said: "Fulan yameed fi mishyatihi," meaning he sways in his walk.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And rivers﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: and He placed in it paths, because the meaning of "alqa" (cast) is "ja'ala" (placed). As for "subul," they are roads. ﴿And that you may be guided﴾ meaning: so that you may be guided to your destinations.

(p-436) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And landmarks﴾. In it there are three views:

One: that they are landmarks of the roads by day, and by the star they are guided by night; narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that they are also the stars; some of them are signs by which one is not guided, and some of them are those by which one is guided; said by Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Nakha'i.

The third: that they are mountains; said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil.

Regarding what is meant by "al-najm" (the star), there are four views:

One: that it is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), the two Farqads, the Great Bear (Banat Na'sh), and the Pole Star (al-Jadi); said by al-Suddi.

The second: that it is the Pole Star (al-Jadi) and the two Farqads; said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third: that it is the Pole Star alone, because it is the most fixed of all the stars in its place; mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The fourth: that it is a collective noun, and what is meant is all the stars; said by al-Zajjaj. Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Yahya ibn Waththab read: ﴿وَبِالنَّجْمِ﴾ with a damma on the nun and sukun on the jim. Al-Jahdari read: "wa-bi-l-nujum" with damma on both the nun and the jim. Mujahid read: "wa-bi-l-nujum" with a waw, in the plural.

Regarding what is meant by this guidance there are two views:

One: guidance to the qibla. The second: guidance to the road during travel.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you see the ships﴾ means: the ships. Regarding the meaning of "mawakhir" (ploughing through), there are two views:

One: they are sailing, as said by Ibn Abbas. The linguists said: it is said "makhara al-safina makhran" when the ship cuts through the water in its course.

The second: "mawaqir" (laden), meaning filled, as said by al-Hasan.

Regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾ there are two views:

One: by riding in it for trade, seeking profit from the bounty of Allah.

The second: by what you extract from its ornaments and hunt from its fish. Ibn al-Anbari said: regarding the entry of the waw (و) in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And that you may seek of His bounty﴾ there are two aspects:

One: that it is conjoined with a deleted lam, its estimation being: "And you see the ships ploughing in it, that you may benefit by that and that you may seek."

The second: that it has entered upon a hidden verb, its estimation being: "And He did that so that you may seek."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And He cast into the earth firm mountains﴾ meaning: He set in it fixed mountains. ﴿Lest it should shake﴾ meaning: so that it would not shake. Al-Zajjaj said: "out of dislike that it should shake." It is said: "madda al-rajul yameed mayadan" when he is turned around with it. Ibn Qutayba said: al-mayd (ميد) is movement and inclination; it is said: "Fulan yameed fi mishyatihi," meaning he sways in his walk.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And rivers﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: and He placed in it paths, because the meaning of "alqa" (cast) is "ja'ala" (placed). As for "subul," they are roads. ﴿And that you may be guided﴾ meaning: so that you may be guided to your destinations.

(p-436) His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And landmarks﴾. In it there are three views:

One: that they are landmarks of the roads by day, and by the star they are guided by night; narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that they are also the stars; some of them are signs by which one is not guided, and some of them are those by which one is guided; said by Mujahid, Qatada, and al-Nakha'i.

The third: that they are mountains; said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil.

Regarding what is meant by "al-najm" (the star), there are four views:

One: that it is the Pleiades (al-Thurayya), the two Farqads, the Great Bear (Banat Na'sh), and the Pole Star (al-Jadi); said by al-Suddi.

The second: that it is the Pole Star (al-Jadi) and the two Farqads; said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The third: that it is the Pole Star alone, because it is the most fixed of all the stars in its place; mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The fourth: that it is a collective noun, and what is meant is all the stars; said by al-Zajjaj. Al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Abu al-Mutawakkil, and Yahya ibn Waththab read: ﴿وَبِالنَّجْمِ﴾ with a damma on the nun and sukun on the jim. Al-Jahdari read: "wa-bi-l-nujum" with damma on both the nun and the jim. Mujahid read: "wa-bi-l-nujum" with a waw, in the plural.

Regarding what is meant by this guidance there are two views:

One: guidance to the qibla. The second: guidance to the road during travel.

(p-437) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is then He who creates like one who creates not?﴾ He means the idols. He referred to them with "man" (who) only because they ascribed to them intellect and discernment. ﴿Will you not then take heed?﴾ means the polytheists: "Will you not then be admonished as the believers were admonished?"

Al-Farra' said: It was permissible to say ﴿like one who creates not﴾ because it was mentioned alongside the Creator, as in His saying: ﴿Among them is one who walks on his belly, and among them is one who walks on two legs﴾ [al-Nur: 45]. The Arabs say: "The rider and his camel became confused for me, so I do not know which is which" (man dha min dha), because when they combined humans and others, "min" (of) was suitable for both of them together.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you were to count the favor of Allah, you could not enumerate it﴾. We have explained this in (Ibrahim: 34).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Forgiving﴾, that is, for what has occurred from you of shortcoming in thanking His favors, ﴿Merciful﴾ toward you, since He has not cut them off from you because of your shortcoming.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah knows what you conceal and what you declare.﴾ 'Abd al-Warith narrated, except al-Qazzaz, "yusirruna" and "yu'linuna" with the letter ya' (third-person form).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 20–21:

His saying, Exalted is He: "And those whom they invoke besides Allah" (wa-alladhina tad'una min duni Allah). ʿĀṣim read yadʿūna with the yāʾ (i.e., "they invoke," in the third person masculine rather than the second person).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿They are dead, not living﴾. He means: the idols. Al-Farrāʾ said: The meaning of "dead" here is that they have no spirit (rūḥ) in them. Al-Akhfash said: His saying "not living" is an emphasis (tawkīd).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they do not perceive when they will be raised﴾. "Ayyāna" (when) here carries the meaning of "matā" (when).

Regarding those referred to (al-mushār ilayhim), there are two opinions:

The first: they are the idols, and He refers to them as He refers to human beings. Ibn ʿAbbās said: (p-438) That is because Allah Exalted will resurrect the idols, which will have spirits, and with them their devils. Then they will disown their worship, and then the devils and those who used to worship them will be commanded to the Fire.

The second: they are the disbelievers, who do not know when they will be resurrected. This was said by Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 20–21:

His saying, Exalted is He: "And those whom they invoke besides Allah" (wa-alladhina tad'una min duni Allah). ʿĀṣim read yadʿūna with the yāʾ (i.e., "they invoke," in the third person masculine rather than the second person).

Then they will disown their worship, and then the devils and those who used to worship them will be commanded to the Fire.

The second: they are the disbelievers, who do not know when they will be resurrected. This was said by Muqatil.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Your God is one God﴾.** We have already discussed it in Surat al-Baqarah (2:163).

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿As for those who do not believe in the Hereafter﴾**, that is, in the Resurrection and the recompense. **﴿Their hearts are denying﴾**, that is, they are rejecting and do not recognize monotheism (tawhid). **﴿And they are arrogant﴾**, that is, they refuse to accept the truth.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Certainly﴾ (la jarama)**. We have explained it in Surat Hud (11:22). The meaning of the verse is that He will repay them for what they conceal and what they reveal, because He knows it. **﴿Those who are arrogant﴾** are those who are haughty toward monotheism and faith. Muqatil said: **﴿What they conceal﴾** refers to when they sent men along every road to turn people away from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, **﴿and what they reveal﴾** refers to when they openly showed enmity toward the Messenger of Allah.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them﴾**, meaning the arrogant ones, **﴿What has your Lord sent down?﴾** upon Muhammad ﷺ. Al-Zajjaj said: "*Madha*" here means "*ma alladhi*" (what is it that). **﴿Tales of the ancients﴾** is in the nominative as the answer. It is as if they said: "What was sent down is the tales of the ancients," meaning: what you claim has been sent down is the tales of the ancients. We have explained the meaning of *asatir* (tales) in Surat al-An'am (6:25). Muqatil said: Those whom al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah sent along the roads of Makkah to turn people away from faith, some of them would say: "Muhammad is a sorcerer," and some would say: "He is a poet." We have explained this meaning in Surat al-Hijr (15:90) in the mention of *al-Muqtasimin* (those who divided the Qur'an).

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full﴾.** This is the *lam al-'aqibah* (the lam of consequence), which we have explained in more than one place. *Awzar* means sins. He said "in full" because nothing of it is expiated for them by whatever calamity or affliction befalls them, as it is expiated for the believer. **﴿And [also] the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾**, that is, they misled them without any evidence. They bear the burdens of the followers because they were leaders who were followed in error. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two aspects regarding *min* (from):

The first: it is partitive (*lil-tab'id*). They bear what they shared with them in, but what those [followers] committed by their own choice, without these [leaders] adorning it for them, they do not bear. So the partitive sense is valid.

The second: *min* is emphatic (*muakkidah*), and the meaning is: *and the burdens of those whom they mislead*. **﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾**, that is, wretched is what they have carried upon their backs.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those before them had plotted﴾.** The exegetes said: it refers to Nimrod ibn Kan'an, because he built a tall tower (*sarh*). They differed about its height. Ibn 'Abbas said it was five thousand cubits, and Muqatil said its height was two farsakh. They said: he intended to ascend to the heavens to fight its inhabitants, according to his claim. The meaning of *makr* (plotting) here is corrupt planning.

There are two opinions regarding the *ha'* and *mim* in *qablihim* (before them):

The first: they refer to those who divided [the Qur'an] regarding the punishment of Makkah. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second: they refer to the disbelievers of Makkah. This was said by Muqatil.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So Allah came to their structure from its foundations﴾**, that is, from its base. The exegetes said: Allah sent a wind which cast the top of the tower into the sea, and what remained fell upon them.

Al-Suddi said: When the tower collapsed, people's tongues were confused from fear, so they spoke seventy-three languages. For this reason it was called *Babil* (Babel). Before that, people's language had been Syriac (*suryaniyyah*). This is a rejected statement, because confusion entails mixing and speaking in something that is not correct. As for it producing a newly created language with well-defined boundaries, that is false. Languages are rather a teaching from Allah, may He be exalted.

If it is said: when the plotter was one person, how did He say "*alladhina*" (those) and not "*alladhi*" (the one)? There are three answers regarding this:

The first: the plotter was a king who had followers, so they were included with him in the description.

The second: the Arabs use the plural for the singular. One of them says: "I went to Basra on mules," though he only went on one mule.

The third: *alladhina* does not refer to one specific person, but it means: *the tyrants before them had plotted*, so the outcome of their plotting was that calamity returned upon them. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these answers. He said: Some scholars mentioned that He only said **﴿from above them﴾** to draw attention to the fact that they were beneath it. For if He had not said that, it would have been possible that they were not beneath it, because the Arabs say: "The house fell upon us," "The shop collapsed upon us," and "The house caved in upon us," and they were not beneath it.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive﴾**, that is, from where they thought they were safe. Al-Suddi said: They were seized from their place of safety. 'Atiyyah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: A punishment fell upon them from the sky. The majority of the exegetes hold to what we have related: that it was a structure which collapsed. Ibn Qutaybah said: This is a parable, and the meaning is: Allah destroyed them, just as one whose dwelling is demolished from its base falls upon him.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them﴾**, that is, He will humiliate them with punishment. **﴿And He will say: "Where are My partners﴾**. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read *shuraka'iya alladhina* with a hamzah and a fatha on the *ya'*. Al-Bazzi reported from Ibn Kathir: *shurakay*, like *huday*. The meaning is: Where are My partners according to your claim? Why did they not defend you? **﴿For whom you used to oppose [Me]﴾**, that is, you used to oppose the Muslims, so you worshipped them while they worshipped Allah. Nafi' read *tushaqqunni* with a kasrah on the *nun*, intending *tushaqqunani* (you oppose Me), and he dropped the second *nun* and left the kasrah to indicate it. The meaning is: you used to contend with Me regarding them, and oppose My command for their sake.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who were given knowledge will say﴾.** Regarding them there are three opinions:

One: they are the angels. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: they are the angels who record deeds (*hafazah*). This was said by Muqatil.

Third: they are the believers.

As for *al-khizy* (disgrace), we have explained it in several places (Ali 'Imran 3:192). And *al-su'* (evil) here means punishment.

Muqatil said: **﴿What they conceal﴾** refers to when they sent men along every road to turn people away from the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, **﴿and what they reveal﴾** refers to when they openly showed enmity toward the Messenger of Allah.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when it is said to them﴾**, meaning the arrogant ones, **﴿What has your Lord sent down?﴾** upon Muhammad ﷺ. Al-Zajjaj said: "*Madha*" here means "*ma alladhi*" (what is it that). **﴿Tales of the ancients﴾** is in the nominative as the answer. It is as if they said: "What was sent down is the tales of the ancients," meaning: what you claim has been sent down is the tales of the ancients. We have explained the meaning of *asatir* (tales) in Surat al-An'am (6:25). Muqatil said: Those whom al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah sent along the roads of Makkah to turn people away from faith, some of them would say: "Muhammad is a sorcerer," and some would say: "He is a poet." We have explained this meaning in Surat al-Hijr (15:90) in the mention of *al-Muqtasimin* (those who divided the Qur'an).

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That they may bear their burdens in full﴾.** This is the *lam al-'aqibah* (the lam of consequence), which we have explained in more than one place. *Awzar* means sins. He said "in full" because nothing of it is expiated for them by whatever calamity or affliction befalls them, as it is expiated for the believer. **﴿And [also] the burdens of those whom they mislead without knowledge﴾**, that is, they misled them without any evidence. They bear the burdens of the followers because they were leaders who were followed in error. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned two aspects regarding *min* (from):

The first: it is partitive (*lil-tab'id*). They bear what they shared with them in, but what those [followers] committed by their own choice, without these [leaders] adorning it for them, they do not bear. So the partitive sense is valid.

The second: *min* is emphatic (*muakkidah*), and the meaning is: *and the burdens of those whom they mislead*. **﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they bear﴾**, that is, wretched is what they have carried upon their backs.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those before them had plotted﴾.** The exegetes said: it refers to Nimrod ibn Kan'an, because he built a tall tower (*sarh*). They differed about its height. Ibn 'Abbas said it was five thousand cubits, and Muqatil said its height was two farsakh. They said: he intended to ascend to the heavens to fight its inhabitants, according to his claim. The meaning of *makr* (plotting) here is corrupt planning.

There are two opinions regarding the *ha'* and *mim* in *qablihim* (before them):

The first: they refer to those who divided [the Qur'an] regarding the punishment of Makkah. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second: they refer to the disbelievers of Makkah. This was said by Muqatil.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So Allah came to their structure from its foundations﴾**, that is, from its base. The exegetes said: Allah sent a wind which cast the top of the tower into the sea, and what remained fell upon them.

Al-Suddi said: When the tower collapsed, people's tongues were confused from fear, so they spoke seventy-three languages. For this reason it was called *Babil* (Babel). Before that, people's language had been Syriac (*suryaniyyah*). This is a rejected statement, because confusion entails mixing and speaking in something that is not correct. As for it producing a newly created language with well-defined boundaries, that is false. Languages are rather a teaching from Allah, may He be exalted.

If it is said: when the plotter was one person, how did He say "*alladhina*" (those) and not "*alladhi*" (the one)? There are three answers regarding this:

The first: the plotter was a king who had followers, so they were included with him in the description.

The second: the Arabs use the plural for the singular. One of them says: "I went to Basra on mules," though he only went on one mule.

The third: *alladhina* does not refer to one specific person, but it means: *the tyrants before them had plotted*, so the outcome of their plotting was that calamity returned upon them. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these answers. He said: Some scholars mentioned that He only said **﴿from above them﴾** to draw attention to the fact that they were beneath it. For if He had not said that, it would have been possible that they were not beneath it, because the Arabs say: "The house fell upon us," "The shop collapsed upon us," and "The house caved in upon us," and they were not beneath it.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the punishment came to them from where they did not perceive﴾**, that is, from where they thought they were safe. Al-Suddi said: They were seized from their place of safety. 'Atiyyah narrated from Ibn 'Abbas who said: A punishment fell upon them from the sky. The majority of the exegetes hold to what we have related: that it was a structure which collapsed. Ibn Qutaybah said: This is a parable, and the meaning is: Allah destroyed them, just as one whose dwelling is demolished from its base falls upon him.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then on the Day of Resurrection He will disgrace them﴾**, that is, He will humiliate them with punishment. **﴿And He will say: "Where are My partners﴾**. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, and al-Kisa'i read *shuraka'iya alladhina* with a hamzah and a fatha on the *ya'*. Al-Bazzi reported from Ibn Kathir: *shurakay*, like *huday*. The meaning is: Where are My partners according to your claim? Why did they not defend you? **﴿For whom you used to oppose [Me]﴾**, that is, you used to oppose the Muslims, so you worshipped them while they worshipped Allah. Nafi' read *tushaqqunni* with a kasrah on the *nun*, intending *tushaqqunani* (you oppose Me), and he dropped the second *nun* and left the kasrah to indicate it. The meaning is: you used to contend with Me regarding them, and oppose My command for their sake.

**His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Those who were given knowledge will say﴾.** Regarding them there are three opinions:

One: they are the angels. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

Second: they are the angels who record deeds (*hafazah*). This was said by Muqatil.

Third: they are the believers.

As for *al-khizy* (disgrace), we have explained it in several places (Ali 'Imran 3:192). And *al-su'* (evil) here means punishment.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 28–29:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those whose souls the angels take while they are wronging themselves﴾. ʿIkrima said: These were a people in Mecca who professed Islam but did not emigrate, so the polytheists took them out against their will to Badr, and some of them were killed. We have explained this in surah al-Nisa' (4:97).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then they will offer submission﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: They submitted and surrendered; al-salam (the submission) means al-istislam (surrender). The exegetes said: This is at the time of death, when they disavow polytheism, and this is their saying: ﴿We did not do any evil﴾, which is polytheism. So the angels reply to them, saying: ﴿Yes indeed﴾. It was also said: This is the reply of the guardians of Hell to them: ﴿Yes indeed, Allah is Knowing of what you used to do﴾ of polytheism and denial. Then it will be said to them: ﴿Enter the gates of Hell to abide therein﴾. The meanings of the words of this verse have already been explained in al-Nisa' (4:97) and al-Hijr (15:44).

The Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 16, verses 30–32:

God's words: ﴿And it will be said to those who were mindful of God, "What has your Lord sent down?"﴾ Abu Salih narrated from Ibn Abbas that "the polytheists of Quraysh sent sixteen men to the passes of Makkah during the days of the Hajj, along the routes of the people, and placed four men at each pass to turn the people away from the Messenger of God (ﷺ). They said to them: 'Whoever comes to you from among the people asking about Muhammad, let some of you say: he is a poet; let some of you say: he is a soothsayer; let some of you say: he is a madman. It is better for you that you neither see him nor let him see you.' When they [the people] reached us, we would confirm what you have said.' This reached the Messenger of God (ﷺ), so he sent to each group of four of them four Muslims, among whom was Abdullah ibn Mas'ud. They were commanded to deny what they said. Whenever people passed by the polytheists and they said what they said, the Muslims would respond to them, saying, 'They have lied. Rather, he calls to the truth, enjoins what is good, forbids what is evil, and calls to goodness.' They would ask, 'What is this goodness to which he calls?' And they would say: ﴿For those who did good in this world, there is good﴾."

God's words: ﴿They said, "Good."﴾ That is, He sent down good. Then He explained that good, saying: ﴿For those who did good in this world﴾, [meaning] they said: There is no god but God, and they did good deeds. ﴿There is good﴾, that is, a noble reward from God the Exalted in the Hereafter, which is Paradise. It was also said: ﴿For those who did good in this world there is good﴾ in this world, which is the provision He gave them of its goodness and their obedience to Him within it. ﴿And the abode of the Hereafter is better﴾, meaning Paradise, ﴿is better﴾ than this world.

Regarding God's words: ﴿And excellent is the abode of those who are mindful of God﴾, there are two opinions:

One: it is Paradise, as the majority said. Ibn al-Anbari (Ibn al-Anbari, a grammarian and commentator) said: there is an omission in the sentence; its sense is: "And excellent is the abode of those who are mindful of God, the Hereafter." However, since it was mentioned first, its meaning is understood at the end. It is also possible that the meaning is: "And excellent is the abode of those who are mindful of God: Gardens of Eden."

The second: it is this world. Al-Hasan said: "And excellent is the abode of those who are mindful of God, the world, because by acting in it they attained the reward of the Hereafter."

God's words: ﴿Gardens of Eden﴾: we have explained it in (Bara'ah: 72).

God's words: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death﴾. Hamzah read yatawaffahum with a ya' and imalah (a vowel-inclining pronunciation). Regarding the meaning of "good" (ṭayyibīn), there are five opinions:

One: believers. The second: pure from polytheism. The third: their deeds and words are pure. The fourth: good at their death, their departure of souls being easy. The fifth: good in their souls regarding death, confident in the reward.

God's words: ﴿saying﴾, meaning the angels: ﴿Peace be upon you﴾.

Regarding when this [greeting of peace] occurs, there are two opinions:

One: at the time of death. Al-Bara' ibn Azib said: the Angel of Death greets him when he enters upon him. Al-Qurazi said: he says to him, "God the Mighty and Majestic sends you peace and gives you the good news of Paradise."

The second: at the entrance into Paradise. Muqatil said: this is the statement of the keepers of Paradise to them in the Hereafter, saying: "Peace be upon you."

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 33–34:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Do they await only that the angels come to them﴾. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "yaʾtiyahum" with a ya' (so the verb is in the third person, "that He comes to them"). This is a threat to the polytheists. We have explained it in (al-Baqarah: 210) and at the end of (al-An'am: 158).

Regarding His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿or that the command of your Lord comes﴾, there are two views:

One: it is God's command concerning them. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it is the punishment in this world. This was said by Muqatil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus did those before them do﴾. He means: the disbelievers of the earlier nations, who denied as these did. ﴿And God did not wrong them﴾ by destroying them, ﴿but they were wronging themselves (p-445)﴾ by associating partners with Him. ﴿So the evil consequences of what they had done struck them﴾, that is, their recompense. Ibn 'Abbas said: the recompense of what they did of polytheism. ﴿And there encompassed them﴾ (this has been explained in al-An'am: 10), and the meaning is: it surrounded them, ﴿what they used to mock﴾ of the punishment.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 35–37:**

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Those who associated partners [with God] said﴾, meaning the disbelievers of Makkah: "If Allah had willed, we would not have worshipped anything besides Him," meaning the idols. That is, if He had willed, we would not have associated partners with Him, nor would we have forbidden, apart from Him, anything of the *bahira* (a she-camel whose ear was slit and released), the *sa'iba* (a animal released to roam freely), the *wasila* (a she-camel or sheep that was held sacred for giving birth to a certain number of young), the *ham* (a stallion camel released after it had served a certain number of mares), or the *harth* (crops set apart for the idols). This was because, when the verse ﴿And you do not will except that Allah wills﴾ (76:30) was revealed, they said this as mockery, not as a matter of belief. It has also been said that the meaning of their words was: "If He had not commanded us to do this and willed it from us, we would not have done it."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Likewise did those before them﴾, that is, they denied the messengers and forbade what Allah had made lawful. ﴿So is there upon the messengers anything but clear notification?﴾ meaning: upon them is only the delivery of the message. As for guidance, it belongs to Allah the Exalted. He explained this by His saying: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger﴾, that is, just as We sent you to these people, ﴿[saying], "Worship Allah and avoid *taghut*"﴾, that is, make Him one, and avoid *taghut* (every object of worship besides Allah), which is Satan. ﴿Among them were those whom Allah guided﴾, that is, He directed them, (p-٤٤٦) ﴿and among them were those upon whom error was decreed﴾, that is, it was made obligatory in the prior knowledge of Allah. Thus Allah the Mighty and Majestic informed that He sent the messengers only to command worship, while misguidance and guidance are from His own will. ﴿So travel through the earth﴾, that is, taking warning from the traces of the nations that denied. Then He affirmed that whoever has error decreed upon him will not be guided, so He said: ﴿If you are eager for their guidance﴾, that is, [if] you seek their guidance with all your effort, ﴿then indeed Allah does not guide those He misguides﴾.

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr, Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir read ﴿لا يُهْدى﴾ ("la yuhda," with a raised *ya'* and an open *dal*), and the meaning is: whomever He misguides, there is no guide for him. ʿĀsim, Hamza and al-Kisa'i read ﴿يَهْدِي﴾ ("yahdi," with an open *ya'* and a kasra on the *dal*). They did not differ regarding ﴿يُضِلُّ﴾ ("yudillu"), which is read with a raised *ya'* and a kasra on the *dad*. This reading (*qira'a*, a recognized mode of Qur'anic recitation) admits two meanings, which Ibn al-Anbari mentioned:

One: He does not guide whom He has made to be astray by nature and created as wretched.

The other: He does not guide, that is, whom Allah misguides does not become guided. So the meaning of *yahdi* here is *yahtadi* (he is guided). The Arabs say: "So-and-so was guided to the road" (*qad hudiya fulan al-tariq*), meaning: he became guided.

His saying ﴿Yes﴾ is a refutation of them. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is, "Yes, He will certainly resurrect them, as a promise binding upon Him, a truth."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so that He may make clear to them that about which they differ﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is permissible for this to be connected to the resurrection, so the meaning would be: "Yes, He will resurrect them, and He will make clear to them." It is also permissible for it to be connected to His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We certainly sent into every nation a messenger﴾, so that He may make clear to them.

Regarding His saying ﴿so that He may make clear to them﴾ the exegetes have two opinions:

The first: they are all of mankind. This was said by Qatadah.

The second: they are the polytheists, to whom He makes clear, through the resurrection, what they opposed the believers about.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that they were liars﴾, i.e., in what they swore to regarding the denial of the resurrection. Then He informed of His power to resurrect by His saying: ﴿Our word to a thing, when We intend it, is only that We say to it, "Be," and it is﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr and Hamza read ﴿fa-yakunu﴾ (and it is) with a final *damma* (raised), and so throughout the Qur'an. Ibn 'Amir and al-Kisa'i read ﴿fa-yakuna﴾ (and it may be) with a final *fatha* (in the subjunctive). Makki ibn Ibrahim said: whoever reads it raised, has cut it off from what precedes it, and the meaning is: "so He is one who brings it about." Whoever reads it in the subjunctive has made it coordinate with ﴿yaqula﴾ (say). This is like His saying: ﴿And when He decrees a matter, He only says to it, "Be," and it is﴾. We explained it in (al-Baqara: 117).

If it is asked: how is a thing called a "thing" before its existence?

The answer: the term "thing" applies to what is known to Allah before creation, because it is like what has already been seen and witnessed.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who emigrated for the cause of Allah﴾. The exegetes differed about who was meant, in three opinions:

(p-448) The first: it was revealed about six of the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ: Bilal, 'Ammar, Suhayb, Khabbab ibn al-Aratt, and 'Ayish and Jabr, two freedmen of the Quraysh, whom the people of Makkah seized and began to torture in order to turn them away from Islam. This was said by Abu Salih, from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it was revealed about Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl ibn 'Amr. This was said by Dawud ibn Abi Hind.

The third: they are all the emigrants among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. This was said by Qatadah. The meaning of ﴿emigrated for the cause of Allah﴾ is: seeking His pleasure and reward. ﴿After they had been wronged﴾ by what the polytheists inflicted upon them. ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good dwelling﴾. Regarding it there are five opinions:

First: "We will surely settle them in Madinah." Abu Salih related this meaning from Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan, al-Sha'bi and Qatadah said likewise. The meaning would then be: "We will surely settle them in a good abode and a good town."

Second: "We will surely provide them in this world with good sustenance." This was said by Mujahid.

Third: victory over the enemy. This was said by al-Dahhak.

Fourth: that what remains after them of good praise, and what passes to their descendants of nobility. Al-Mawardi mentioned this. Its meaning has also been related from Mujahid: Ibn Abi Najih reported from him that he said regarding ﴿We will surely settle them in this world in a good dwelling﴾: "a true tongue (good reputation)."

Fifth: the meaning is: "We will surely be good to them in this world." Some of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: on these opinions, ﴿We will surely settle them﴾ is figurative (isti'ara), except on the first opinion.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the reward of the Hereafter is greater, if they only knew﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: "It means Paradise." ﴿If they only knew﴾ means the people of Makkah.

It is related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that whenever he gave a man from among the (p-449) emigrants his stipend, he would say: "Take it; may Allah bless it for you. This is what Allah has promised you in this world, and what He has stored up for you in the Hereafter is better," and then he would recite this verse.

Then Allah praised them and commended them for their patience, saying: ﴿Those who were patient﴾, i.e., in their religion; they did not abandon it because of any harm they suffered, and in all of that they trusted in their Lord.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 43–44:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We did not send before you except men﴾. The exegetes (mufassirun) said: When the polytheists of Quraysh denied the prophethood of Muhammad (ﷺ) and said: "God is too great for His messenger to be a human being; why did He not send an angel to us?", this verse was revealed. The meaning is: the messengers were before you human beings like you, except that revelation was sent to them. Hafs, from ʿAsim, recited "nūḥī" with the nun and with a kasra on the ḥa'. ﴿So ask﴾, O assembly of polytheists, ﴿the people of the reminder (ahl al-dhikr)﴾, and regarding them there are four opinions:

The first: they are the people of the Torah and the Gospel; this was said by Abu Salih from Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: the people of the Torah; this was said by Mujahid. The third: the people of the Qur'an; this was said by Ibn Zayd. The fourth: the scholars of the reports of those who came before; this was mentioned by al-Mawardi.

As for His saying, the Exalted: ﴿if you do not know﴾, there are two views:

One of them: you do not know that God the Exalted sent a messenger from among humans.

The second: you do not know that Muhammad is the messenger of God. According to the first view, it is permissible to ask both those who believe in the messenger of God and those who disbelieve, because the people of the Book and the people knowledgeable in histories agree that all the prophets were human. According to the second view, one asks only those among the People of the Book who believe. It has been narrated from Mujahid regarding ﴿ask the people of the reminder﴾ that he said: ʿAbd Allah ibn Salam; and from Qatada, who said: Salman al-Farisi.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿with clear proofs and the scriptures﴾. Regarding this "bi" (with) there are two views:

One of them: in the speech there is an inversion (taqdim wa ta'khir), its sense being: "We did not send before you except men whom We sent with clear proofs." And az-Zubur: the books. We have explained this in (Al ʿImran: 184).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Reminder﴾, which is the Qur'an by the consensus of the exegetes, ﴿so that you may make clear to the people what has been sent down to them﴾ [in it] of lawful and unlawful, and promise and warning, ﴿and that they may reflect﴾ upon that, so that they may take heed.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 45–47:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do those who devised evil deeds feel secure﴾. The exegetes said: He meant the polytheists of Makkah. Their devising of evil deeds is their polytheism and their denial. It was called "devising" (makr) because makr in the language means striving toward corruption (al-sa'y bi'l-fasad). This is a rhetorical question of denial, and its meaning is: they should not feel secure from punishment. Mujahid used to say: by this speech he meant Nimrod ibn Kan'an.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or that He will seize them in their going back and forth﴾. Regarding this there are four opinions:

The first: in their journeys. This was related by al-Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas, and Qatadah said likewise.

The second: in their sleep. This was related by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: in their night and their day. This was said by al-Dahhak, Ibn Jurayj, and Muqatil.

The fourth: that it refers to everything in which they move about. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or that He will seize them with gradual decline (ʿalā takhawwuf)﴾. Regarding this there are two opinions:

The first: "upon gradual decline" (ʿalā tanaqqus). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, and al-Dahhak. Ibn Qutaybah said: takhawwuf means tanaqqus (diminution), and its like is takhawwun. It is said: "the ages diminished him (takhawwafathu al-duhur) and took from him (takhawwanathu)," when they diminish him and take from his wealth and body. Al-Haytham ibn 'Adi said: takhawwuf means tanaqqus, in the dialect of the Azd Shanu'ah.

Then within this diminution there are three opinions: the first, that it is a diminution of their deeds, related by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The second, that it is seizing them one after another, related from Ibn 'Abbas as well. The third, that it is the diminution of their wealth and crops until He destroys them, said by al-Zajjaj.

The second: that takhawwuf itself is the meaning, and within it there are two opinions: the first, that He seizes them while in fear that He may punish or pass over them, said by Qatadah. The second, that He seizes one town so that the other town is frightened, said by al-Dahhak. Al-Zajjaj said: He seizes them after frightening them by destroying a town so that the one next to it becomes afraid. According to this, He frightened them before their destruction, and they did not repent, so they deserved the punishment.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed your Lord is Kind and Merciful﴾, since He did not hasten the punishment and granted respite for repentance.

(p-٤٥٢) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have they not seen﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "Awalam yaraw" with the ya' (they). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "Tarawa" with the ta' (you). The reading transmitted from 'Asim varies.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿to anything that Allah has created﴾. He means anything that has a shadow: a mountain, a tree, or an upright body. The majority read "yatafayya'u" with the ya'. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with the ta', "zilaluhu" (its shadows). "Zilal" is the plural of "zill" (shadow). It is pluralized although it is attached to a singular noun, because the singular is intended to express abundance, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that you may sit firmly upon its back﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 13]. Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning of "yatafayya'u zilaluhu" is that it turns and returns from one side to the other. "Fay'" means return, and from it the shadow in the evening is called "fay'", because it has returned from the west to the east. The exegetes said: When the sun rises while you are facing the qibla, the shadow is in front of you. When it rises higher, it is on your right. After that, it is behind you. When it approaches sunset, it is on your left. The word "right" (al-yamin) is used in the singular, though the plural is intended, for brevity of expression, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45]. The word "left" (ash-shama'il) in the plural indicates that the plural is intended. Al-Farra' said: He used the singular for "right" and the plural for "left", and did not say "ash-shimal", because all of this is permissible in the language. He recited:

The arrivers and Taym at the heights of Saba,
the hides of buffaloes have bitten their necks.

He did not say "julud" (hides, plural). A similar example is:

Eat from the middle of your belly and you will live,
for your time is a lean time.

The singular was permitted because most speech is addressed to the singular.

(p-٤٥٣) Others said: "The right" refers to the word "ma" (anything), which is singular, while "the lefts" refers to the meaning, which is plural.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿prostrating to Allah﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: submissive and obedient. We explained this meaning at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and their shadows in the mornings and evenings﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 15].

Regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿while they are humbled﴾, there are two opinions:
One: the unbelievers are humiliated.
The second: these things are humbled, created to obey. Al-Akhfash said: He used the masculine for those who are not human because, when He described them as obedient, they resembled humans in their action.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And to Allah prostrates whatever is in the heavens...﴾, the verse. Those who prostrate are of two kinds:
One: those who have intellect, whose prostration is worship.
The second: those who lack intellect, whose prostration shows the effect of the craftsmanship in them, and the submission that indicates they are created. This is the view of a group of scholars, who argued with the words of the poet:

With an army in whose sides the spotted horses lose their way,
you see the hills in it prostrate before the hooves.

(p-٤٥٤) Ibn Qutayba said: "Hajarat" means its sides. He means that the hooves of the horses have uprooted the hills and trampled them until they were humbled and lowered. As for the sun, the moon and the stars, a group counted them among those who have intellect. Abu al-'Aliya said: Their prostration is real. None of them sets without falling prostrate before Allah, the Mighty and Majestic, and then it does not turn back until it is given permission. Supporting Abu al-'Aliya's view is the hadith of Abu Dharr, who said: "I was with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the mosque when the sun set. He said: 'O Abu Dharr! Do you know where the sun went?' I said: 'Allah and His Messenger know best.' He said: 'It goes until it prostrates before its Lord, the Mighty and Majestic. Then it asks permission to return, and permission is given to it. It is as if it is said to it: Return from where you came. So it returns to its rising place, and that is its resting place.' Then he recited: ﴿And the sun runs to its resting place﴾ [Ya-Sin: 38]." Related by al-Bukhari and Muslim.

As for plants and trees, their prostration can be one of four things:
One: a prostration we do not know of, if we say that Allah gives them understanding.
The second: that it is the turning of their shadows.
The third: the showing of the craftsmanship in them.
The fourth: submission to what they have been subjected to.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the angels﴾. He singled out the angels from the moving creatures because, by having wings, they are outside the description of crawling.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And they are not arrogant﴾ ﴿They fear their Lord above them and do what they are commanded﴾, there are two opinions:
One: that this is a description of the angels only. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil.
The second: that it is general to all those mentioned. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

(p-٤٥٥) Regarding His saying: ﴿above them﴾, there are two opinions, which Ibn al-Anbari mentioned:
One: that it is praise of Allah, the Exalted, and magnification of His majesty. Its summary: they fear their Lord, who is high, exalted and great.
The second: that it is a circumstance (ḥāl). Its summary: they fear their Lord, glorifying Him, knowing the greatness of His authority.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And the angels﴾. He singled out the angels from the moving creatures because, by having wings, they are outside the description of crawling.

One: that this is a description of the angels only. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil.
The second: that it is general to all those mentioned. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

(p-٤٥٢) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Have they not seen﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', Abu 'Amr and Ibn 'Amir read "Awalam yaraw" with the ya' (they). Hamza and al-Kisa'i read "Tarawa" with the ta' (you). The reading transmitted from 'Asim varies.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿to anything that Allah has created﴾. He means anything that has a shadow: a mountain, a tree, or an upright body. The majority read "yatafayya'u" with the ya'. Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with the ta', "zilaluhu" (its shadows). "Zilal" is the plural of "zill" (shadow). It is pluralized although it is attached to a singular noun, because the singular is intended to express abundance, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that you may sit firmly upon its back﴾ [az-Zukhruf: 13]. Ibn Qutayba said: The meaning of "yatafayya'u zilaluhu" is that it turns and returns from one side to the other. "Fay'" means return, and from it the shadow in the evening is called "fay'", because it has returned from the west to the east. The exegetes said: When the sun rises while you are facing the qibla, the shadow is in front of you. When it rises higher, it is on your right. After that, it is behind you. When it approaches sunset, it is on your left. The word "right" (al-yamin) is used in the singular, though the plural is intended, for brevity of expression, as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and they turn their backs﴾ [al-Qamar: 45]. The word "left" (ash-shama'il) in the plural indicates that the plural is intended. Al-Farra' said: He used the singular for "right" and the plural for "left", and did not say "ash-shimal", because all of this is permissible in the language. He recited:

The arrivers and Taym at the heights of Saba,
the hides of buffaloes have bitten their necks.

He did not say "julud" (hides, plural). A similar example is:

Eat from the middle of your belly and you will live,
for your time is a lean time.

The singular was permitted because most speech is addressed to the singular.

(p-٤٥٣) Others said: "The right" refers to the word "ma" (anything), which is singular, while "the lefts" refers to the meaning, which is plural.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿prostrating to Allah﴾. Ibn Qutayba said: submissive and obedient. We explained this meaning at His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿and their shadows in the mornings and evenings﴾ [ar-Ra'd: 15].

Regarding His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿while they are humbled﴾, there are two opinions:
One: the unbelievers are humiliated.
The second: these things are humbled, created to obey. Al-Akhfash said: He used the masculine for those who are not human because, when He described them as obedient, they resembled humans in their action.

With an army in whose sides the spotted horses lose their way,

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 16, verses 51–52:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah said: Do not take two gods; He is only one God﴾. The occasion of its revelation: a man from among the Muslims called upon Allah in his prayer and called upon "the Most Merciful" (al-Rahman). A man from among the polytheists said: "Does not Muhammad and his companions claim that they worship one Lord? Then what is the matter with this one, calling upon two lords?" So this verse was revealed. This was related by Muqatil. Al-Zajjaj said: The mention of "two" is for emphasis, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Indeed, He is but one God﴾.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And to Him belongs religion, perpetually﴾. Regarding the meaning of "religion" (al-din) there are four opinions:

The first: that it is sincerity (al-ikhlas), related by Mujahid. The second: that it is worship (al-ibadah), related by Sa'id ibn Jubayr.

The third: the testimony that there is no god but Allah, and the establishment of the prescribed punishments (hudud) and obligations (fara'id), related by Ikrimah. The fourth: obedience (al-ta'ah), related by Ibn Qutaybah.

Regarding the meaning of "perpetually" (wasiban) there are four opinions:

The first: "always" (da'iman), related by Ibn Abi Talha from Ibn Abbas. This was also the view of al-Hasan, Ikrimah, Mujahid, al-Dahhak, Qatadah, Ibn Zayd, al-Thawri, and the lexicographers. Abu al-Aswad al-Du'ali said:

I do not seek praise, whose endurance is short,
for a day, by blaming fate entirely, perpetually.

Ibn Qutaybah said: The meaning of the statement is that there is no one to whom obedience is owed and who is obeyed except that this ends for him through cessation or destruction, other than Allah, Mighty and Majestic, for obedience to Him endures.

The second: "obligatory" (wajiban), related by Ikrimah from Ibn Abbas.

The third: "sincere" (khalisan), said by al-Rabi' ibn Anas.

The fourth: "and to Him belongs religion, causing fatigue" (mūsiban), meaning causing weariness, because the truth is heavy. This is like the Arabs' saying: "a worrying concern" (hamm nasib), meaning one that causes fatigue. Al-Nabighah said:

Leave me to a concern, O Umayma, that causes weariness,
and a night I endure, whose stars move slowly.

Ibn al-Anbari mentioned this. Al-Zajjaj said: It is also possible that the meaning is: to Him belongs the religion and the obedience. Whether the servant is content with what he is commanded and it is easy for him, or it is not easy, religion still belongs to Him, even though there may be weariness in it. "Wasab" (weariness) means severe fatigue.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 53–55:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whatever good you have is from Allah﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: whatever blessing has come to you, whether health of body, abundance of provision, or enjoyment of wealth and children, ﴿it is from Allah﴾. Ibn Abi Abla recited: "famannu Allahi" (fa-mannu Allahi), with the nun doubled (tashdid).

(p-457) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then when harm touches you﴾. Ibn Abbas said: He means sicknesses, diseases, and need.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿then to Him you cry out for help﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "tajarun" means you raise your voices to Him in seeking relief. It is said: ja'ara yaj'aru ju'aran. Voice-sounds are patterned on the forms fu'al and fa'il. The fu'al form is like "al-sarakh" (shouting) and "al-khuwar" (lowing), while the fa'il form is like "al-'awil" (wailing) and "al-za'ir" (roaring). The fu'al form is more common.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then, when a party among you﴾. Ibn Abbas said: He means the people of hypocrisy. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: He means the disbelievers.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so that they may disbelieve in what We have given them﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is: so that they disbelieve regarding the fact that We bestowed blessings upon them, so they make Our blessings a means to disbelief. This is like His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Our Lord, You have given Pharaoh...﴾ up to His saying: ﴿so that they may lead [people] astray from Your way﴾ [Yunus: 88]. It is also permissible that "li-yakfuru" means that they deny the blessing of Allah in that matter.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So enjoy yourselves﴾ is a threat, and ﴿you will soon know﴾ the outcome of your affair.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 56–59:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they assign to what they do not know﴾ means: the idols.

Regarding "those who do not know," there are two opinions:

(p-458) The first: they are the ones who assign, namely the polytheists, and the meaning is: "for what they do not know to have any harm or benefit." So the object of knowledge (ʿilm) is omitted, and its estimated sense is: "what we have said." This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: they are the idols, which have no knowledge of anything, no sense perception and no understanding. He said "they know" (yaʿlamūn) because, when they attributed understanding to them, He treated them as beings that reason according to their own assumption. This was said by a group of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-maʿani). The exegetes said: these are the polytheists of the Arabs, who assigned to their idols a portion of their wealth, such as the baḥīrah, the sāʾibah and other things, which we have explained in (al-Anʿam: 139).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿By God, you will certainly be questioned﴾ He turns from speaking about them to addressing them directly, and this is a question of rebuke.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they assign to God daughters﴾ The exegetes said: it means Khuzaʿah and Kinanah, who claimed that the angels are God's daughters. ﴿Glory be to Him﴾ meaning: He is exalted above what they claim. ﴿And for themselves is what they desire﴾ meaning: sons. Abu Sulayman said: the meaning is that they wish for males for themselves.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When one of them is given good news of a female﴾ meaning: he is informed that a daughter has been born to him. ﴿His face becomes dark﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: that is, changed, with the change of one distressed. It is said of everyone who meets with something disliked: "his face has blackened with grief and sorrow."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿while he suppresses (grief)﴾ meaning: he restrains the intensity of his anguish, so he does not show it. We have explained it in Surah Yusuf: 84.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He hides himself from the people﴾ The exegetes said: this was the practice of the polytheists of the Arabs; when a woman's labor pains came upon one of them, he would hide until he learned what was born to him. If it was a male, he was pleased with it; and if it was a female, he would not appear for days, deliberating how to deal with the matter. This is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Will he keep it in humiliation?﴾ The pronoun refers to what is in His saying: ﴿what he was given good news of﴾, and "al-hawn" in the speech of the Arabs means humiliation. Ibn Masʿud, Ibn Abi ʿAbalah and al-Jahdari read: "ʿalā hawān" (in humiliation). "Al-dass" means concealing a thing within a thing, and they used to bury the daughter while she was alive. ﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they decide﴾, in that they assigned to God daughters, of whom their own standing is this, and attributed it to offspring, while they assigned to themselves sons.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 56–59:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they assign to what they do not know﴾ means: the idols.

Regarding "those who do not know," there are two opinions:

(p-458) The first: they are the ones who assign, namely the polytheists, and the meaning is: "for what they do not know to have any harm or benefit." So the object of knowledge (ʿilm) is omitted, and its estimated sense is: "what we have said." This is the view of Mujahid and Qatadah.

The second: they are the idols, which have no knowledge of anything, no sense perception and no understanding. He said "they know" (yaʿlamūn) because, when they attributed understanding to them, He treated them as beings that reason according to their own assumption. This was said by a group of the scholars of meanings (ahl al-maʿani). The exegetes said: these are the polytheists of the Arabs, who assigned to their idols a portion of their wealth, such as the baḥīrah, the sāʾibah and other things, which we have explained in (al-Anʿam: 139).

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿By God, you will certainly be questioned﴾ He turns from speaking about them to addressing them directly, and this is a question of rebuke.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they assign to God daughters﴾ The exegetes said: it means Khuzaʿah and Kinanah, who claimed that the angels are God's daughters. ﴿Glory be to Him﴾ meaning: He is exalted above what they claim. ﴿And for themselves is what they desire﴾ meaning: sons. Abu Sulayman said: the meaning is that they wish for males for themselves.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿When one of them is given good news of a female﴾ meaning: he is informed that a daughter has been born to him. ﴿His face becomes dark﴾ Al-Zajjaj said: that is, changed, with the change of one distressed. It is said of everyone who meets with something disliked: "his face has blackened with grief and sorrow."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿while he suppresses (grief)﴾ meaning: he restrains the intensity of his anguish, so he does not show it. We have explained it in Surah Yusuf: 84.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿He hides himself from the people﴾ The exegetes said: this was the practice of the polytheists of the Arabs; when a woman's labor pains came upon one of them, he would hide until he learned what was born to him. If it was a male, he was pleased with it; and if it was a female, he would not appear for days, deliberating how to deal with the matter. This is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Will he keep it in humiliation?﴾ The pronoun refers to what is in His saying: ﴿what he was given good news of﴾, and "al-hawn" in the speech of the Arabs means humiliation. Ibn Masʿud, Ibn Abi ʿAbalah and al-Jahdari read: "ʿalā hawān" (in humiliation). "Al-dass" means concealing a thing within a thing, and they used to bury the daughter while she was alive. ﴿Unquestionably, evil is what they decide﴾, in that they assigned to God daughters, of whom their own standing is this, and attributed it to offspring, while they assigned to themselves sons.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 60:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For those who do not believe in the Hereafter is the evil likeness﴾, meaning: the evil attribute, from their need for offspring and their aversion to females, out of fear of poverty and shame. ﴿And to Allah belongs the highest likeness﴾, meaning: the highest attribute, from His transcendence and His freedom from having offspring.

Allah's saying: ﴿And if Allah were to seize mankind for their wrongdoing﴾ — meaning, for their polytheism and their sins: whenever anything of it is found among them, they would be seized for it. ﴿He would not leave upon it (ma taraka ʿala ẓahriha)⌋ — "upon it" meaning the earth. This is a kināya (allusive reference) to something not mentioned, yet it is understood, since the creatures that move (al-dawabb) are only upon the earth.

Regarding His saying ﴿any creature (min dabbah)﴾ there are three opinions:

One: that it refers to everything that crawls upon the face of the earth. This was said by Ibn Masʿud. Qatadah said: "He did this in the time of Nuh, peace be upon him." As-Suddi said: "The meaning is that He would withhold the rain, so no creature would remain except that it would perish." Muqatil went to a similar view.

The second: that it intends only mankind. This was said by Ibn Jurayj.

The third: that it means humans and jinn. This was said by Ibn as-Sa'ib, and it is the preference of az-Zajjaj.

Allah's saying: ﴿But He defers them until a specified term﴾ — and this is the end of their appointed lifetimes. The rest of the verse has already been discussed (in al-Aʿraf: 34).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And they assign to Allah what they dislike﴾. The meaning: they judge for Him what they themselves dislike, namely daughters. ﴿And their tongues utter the lie﴾, that is, they say the lie. Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Nakha'i and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *al-kudhub* (الكُذُبُ), with a damma on the *kaf* and the *dhal*. Then he explained that lie by His saying: ﴿That for them is the best﴾. Regarding it there are three opinions:

First: it refers to sons. This was said by Mujahid, Qatadah and Muqatil.

Second: it refers to the good recompense from Allah, Exalted is He. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

Third: [it refers to] Paradise. That is because when Allah promised the believers Paradise, the polytheists said: "If what you say is true, we will surely enter it before you." This was mentioned by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Without doubt (*la jarama*)﴾. We have explained it previously (Hud: 22). Al-Zajjaj said: "*la*" is a rejection of their saying. The meaning is: it is not as they described. "*Jarama*" means: their deed has earned, i.e., their action has merited, that "for them is the Fire and that they are *mufrutun*." In this there are four aspects. Most readers recited ﴿*mufrutun*﴾ with a sukun on the *fa'*, a light *ra'*, and a fatha on the *ra'*. Regarding its meaning there are two opinions:

First: *mutrakun* (abandoned/left behind). This was said by Ibn 'Abbas. al-Farra' said: forgotten in the Fire.

Second: *mu'ajjalun* (hastened/sent ahead). This was also said by Ibn 'Abbas. Ibn Qutaybah said: hastened to the Fire. al-Zajjaj said: the meaning of *al-fark* in the language is "that which precedes," so the meaning of *mufrutun* is "sent ahead to the Fire." Whoever explained it as *mutrakun* also means this, i.e., they have been made to precede to punishment forever, left in it.

Nafi', Mahbub (from Abu 'Amr), and Qutaybah (from al-Kisa'i) read *mufrituun* (مُفْرِطُونَ) with a sukun on the *fa'*, a kasra on the *ra'*, and a light pronunciation. al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that they exceeded the bounds in disobeying Allah.

Abu Ja'far and Ibn Abi 'Ablah read *mufarrituun* (مُفَرِّطُونَ) with a fatha on the *fa'*, a shadda on the *ra'*, and a kasra on it. al-Zajjaj said: its meaning is that they neglected (*farrathu*) in this world, so they did not act in it for the Hereafter. The confirmation of this reading is His saying: ﴿Alas for my regret over what I neglected concerning Allah﴾ (al-Zumar: 56).

al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated from Ibn 'Amir *mufarratun* (مُفَرَّطُونَ) with a fatha on the *fa'* and the *ra'*, and a shadda on it. al-Zajjaj said: its explanation is like the explanation of the first reading, so *al-mufarrat* and *al-mufrat* have one meaning.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 63–64:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿By God, We certainly sent [messengers] to nations before you﴾. The exegetes said: this is a consolation to the Prophet ﷺ. ﴿So Satan made their deeds appear attractive to them﴾, the evil deeds, until they disobeyed and denied. ﴿He is their guardian today﴾. In this there are two opinions:

The first: that it refers to the Day of Resurrection. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil, as if they meant: he is their guardian on the day when the Fire will be theirs.

The second: that it refers to the world, so the meaning is: he is their ally in this world. ﴿And for them is a painful punishment﴾ in the Hereafter. This was said by Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Except that you may make clear to them﴾, meaning: the disbelievers, ﴿that about which they differ﴾, i.e., what they differed with the believers about, of monotheism, resurrection, and recompense. The meaning is: We sent it down as an explanation of that over which disagreement has occurred.
