Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 65–67:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah sends down water from the sky﴾, meaning: rain. ﴿And gives life thereby to the earth after its death﴾, i.e., after its drying up. ﴿Indeed, in that is a sign for a people who hear﴾, i.e., who take heed (ya'tabirun).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And indeed, for you in the livestock is a lesson. We give you drink﴾. Abu 'Amr, Ibn Kathir, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "nusqikum" with a ḍammah on the nun, and the same occurs in (al-Mu'minun: 21). Nafi', Ibn 'Amir and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim recited "naskiyakum" with a fatḥah on the nun in both places. Abu Ja'far recited "tuskikum" with an open tā', and likewise in (al-Mu'minun: 21). The explanation of "al-an'am" has already passed. We have mentioned the meaning of "al-'ibrah" (lesson) in (Al 'Imran: 13), and the difference between "saqa" and "asqa" in (al-Hijr: 22).

As for His saying: ﴿from what is in their bellies﴾, al-Farra' said: "al-ni'am" and "al-an'am" are one thing, and both are plurals, so the masculine pronoun refers back to the meaning of "al-ni'am," since it conveys the sense of "al-an'am." Someone recited to me:

"And the milk of the she-camels was good and cool"

So it returned to "al-laban" (milk), because "al-laban" and "al-alban" have the same meaning. He said: al-Kisa'i said: he intended: "We give you drink from what is in the bellies of what we have mentioned," and this is correct. Someone recited to me:

"Like young birds whose crops have been plucked"

Al-Mubarrad said: this is common in the Qur'an, like His saying to the sun: ﴿This is my Lord﴾ [al-An'am: 78], meaning: this thing rising. Likewise: ﴿And indeed I am sending a gift to them﴾, then He said: ﴿So when it came to Sulayman﴾ [al-Naml: 35–36], and He did not say "came" (feminine), because the meaning is: the thing we mentioned came. Abu 'Ubaydah said: the pronoun in "buṭūnihi" refers to a part (of the livestock), and the meaning is: We give you drink from what is in the bellies of that part which has milk, because not all livestock produce milk. Ibn Qutaybah said: by His saying "mimmā fī buṭūnihi" He intended the ni'am, and ni'am may be treated as masculine or feminine. Al-farth is what is in the stomach (karsh), and the meaning is: milk was food, and from that food blood was separated, and from it remained farth in the stomach, and from that blood came forth ﴿pure milk, palatable to drinkers﴾, i.e., easy to drink, which does not choke its drinker nor cause him to gag. Some said: "sa'ighan" means that the soul does not reject it, even though it has come out from between farth and blood. Abu Salih narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: When the fodder settles in the stomach, it grinds it, so its lowest part becomes farth, its upper part becomes blood, and its middle part becomes milk; the liver is set over these three kinds, so the blood flows in the veins, the milk in the udder, and the farth remains in the stomach.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And from the fruits of the date palms and grapes﴾. The sentence is estimated as: "And for you from the fruits of the date palms and grapes is that from which you take intoxicant (sakar)." The Arabs omit "mā," as in His saying: ﴿And when you see there﴾ [al-Insan: 20], meaning: what is there. The pronoun in "minhu" refers back to the omitted "mā." Al-Akhfash said: He did not say "minhumā" (from both) because He implied a thing, as if He said: "And from them is a thing from which you take intoxicant."

Regarding the meaning of "sakar" there are three opinions:

One: that it is intoxicant (khamr). This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Umar, al-Hasan, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, Ibrahim ibn Abi Layla, al-Zajjaj and Ibn Qutaybah. 'Amr ibn Sufyan narrated from Ibn 'Abbas: "Sakar is what has been forbidden of its fruit." These exegetes said: this verse was revealed when intoxicants were permitted, then [that] was abrogated by His saying: ﴿So avoid it﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 90]. Among those who stated that it is abrogated were Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi and al-Nakha'i.

The second: that "sakar" is vinegar (khall), in the language of Abyssinia, narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas. al-Dahhak said: it is vinegar in the language of Yemen.

The third: that "sakar" is taste (ṭu'm). It is said: "This has sakar for him," i.e., taste. They recited:

"You made the faults of the noble into sakar"

Abu 'Ubaydah said this. According to these two opinions, the verse is muhkam (definitive, not abrogated). As for "ar-rizq al-hasan" (good provision), it is what is permitted from both, such as dates, grapes, raisins, vinegar and the like.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 68–69:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And your Lord inspired to the bee﴾. Regarding this inspiration there are two opinions.

One: It is inspiration (ilham), narrated by al-Dahhak from Ibn Abbas, and this is the view of Mujahid, al-Dahhak, and Muqatil.

The second: It is a command, narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas. Ibn Mujahid narrated from his father that he said: "He sent (it) to them." The nahl (bee) is the wasps of honey, its singular being nahlah. ﴿Yaʿrishun﴾ means they make it into trellises (ʿarish). Ibn Amir and Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read "yaʿrushun" with a damma on the ra', and both are dialects: it is said "yaʿrishu" and "yaʿrushu," like "yaʿkifu" and "yaʿkufu." Then there are two opinions concerning it:

One: "What they trellis" refers to vines, as said by Ibn Zayd.

The second: It refers to the roofs of houses, as said by al-Farra'. Ibn Qutaybah said: Everything that is trellised, whether a vine, a plant, or a roof, is called ʿarsh and maʿrush. It was also said: What is meant by "what they trellis" is the places they build for them in which they deposit the honey, and were it not for the subjection, they would not dwell in them.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Then eat from all the fruits﴾. Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 70:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And Allah created you﴾, meaning: brought you into existence when you were nothing. ﴿Then He causes you to die﴾ at the end of your terms. ﴿And among you is one who is returned to the most abject age﴾, which is its most wretched and lowest state, the state of senility (haram). Regarding its number of years there are three opinions:

The first: seventy-five years, said by ʿAli, peace be upon him. The second: ninety years, said by Qatadah. The third: eighty years, said by Qutrub.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So that he will not know, after knowing, anything﴾. Al-Farra' said: so that he will not understand anything after his former understanding. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, so that he will not know anything after his knowledge of affairs, because of the severity of his senility. Al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is that among you is one who grows old until his intellect departs from him through dementia (kharaf), (p-468) so that he becomes, after having been knowledgeable, ignorant, in order to show you of His power, just as He has power over causing you to die and giving you life, that He is able to transfer him from knowledge to ignorance. ʿAtaʾ related from Ibn ʿAbbas that he said: This does not apply to Muslims; the Muslim does not increase in length of life and endurance except in honour with Allah, and in intellect and knowledge. ʿIkrimah said: whoever recites the Qur'an will not be returned to the most abject age.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 71:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Allah has favoured some of you over others in provision﴾. He means: He has favoured the masters (sayyid, pl. sadah) over the slaves (mamalik). ﴿So those who have been favoured do not give their provision to those whom their right hands possess﴾. He means: the masters. ﴿So that they become equal in it﴾ is not stated here; instead the verse reads: ﴿…so that they would be equal in it with them﴾ is not the wording, and the phrase "ma" (what) is used in place of "man" (those who), because it is a place of ambiguity (ibhām). You say: "What is in the house?" and the addressee replies: "Two men or three." The meaning of the verse is that the master does not return to what his right hand possesses from his wealth such that the master and the slave would be equal in the wealth. This is a parable that Allah, Exalted is He, struck for the polytheists who made the idols partners with Him, and the idols as His property. He says: If your slaves are not equal with you in ownership, how do you make My slaves equal with Me? And do you approve for Me what you disdain for yourselves?

Al-Awfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: They did not make their slaves partners with them in their wealth and their women, so how do they make My slaves partners with Me in My dominion?

Abu Salih reported from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: It was revealed concerning the Christians of Najran when they said: ʿIsa is the son of Allah, Exalted is He.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then do they deny the favour of Allah?﴾ Abu Bakr, from ʿAsim, read "tajhadun" with the letter taʾ. Regarding this favour there are two views:

One: it is His proof and His guidance. The second: it is His bounty and His provision.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 72–74:

(p-469) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah has made for you spouses from among yourselves﴾ — meaning, women.

Regarding the meaning of ﴿from among yourselves﴾ there are two opinions:

One: that He created Adam, then created his wife from him. This is the view of Qatadah.

The second: "from among yourselves," i.e., from your own kind, from the sons of Adam. This is the view of Ibn Zayd.

Regarding al-hafadah (the grandchildren/helpers) there are five opinions:

The first: that they are the in-laws (akhtan), a man's sons-in-law through his daughters. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, by Ibn Abbas in one narration, by Mujahid in one narration, by Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and by al-Nakha'i. They recited in support of this:

"Had my own soul obeyed me, it would have made for me a hafad of many, to be counted,
But it is a soul proud against me, disgusted by the in-laws of the base, repelling."

The second: that they are servants (khadam). This was narrated by Mujahid from Ibn Abbas, and Mujahid also said it in one narration from al-Hasan; likewise Tawus, and Ikrimah in a narration from al-Dahhak. This view admits of two meanings. One: that by the servants is meant the children, so the meaning is that the children serve. Ibn Qutaybah said: al-hafadah are the servants and helpers; so the meaning is that they are sons and they are servants. The root of al-hafd is hasting the step and quickening the walk, and servants do this, so they were called hafadah. From this comes the phrase in the supplication of Witr: "And to You we strive and hasten (nahfid)." The second: that by the servants are meant the slaves, so the meaning of the verse is: He made for you sons from your spouses, and He made for you hafadah other than spouses. This was mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

The third: that they are the sons of a man's wife by another husband. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas, and al-Dahhak said likewise.

The fourth: that they are the children of children (grandchildren). This was narrated by Mujahid from Ibn Abbas.

The fifth: that they are the elder children, and the "sons" are the young ones. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil. Muqatil said: In the Jahiliyyah their children used to serve them. Al-Zajjaj said: The true sense of this speech is that Allah, Exalted, made from the spouses sons, and those who help with what is needed quickly and obediently.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿and provided you with good things﴾. Ibn Abbas said: He means: of the kinds of fruits, grains and livestock.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿Will they then believe in falsehood?﴾ Regarding this there are three opinions:

One: that it refers to the idols. This was said by Ibn Abbas.

The second: that it refers to the partner, the consort and the offspring, so the meaning is: Do they affirm that Allah has these? This was said by Ata'.

The third: that it refers to Satan, who ordered them to forbid the bahirah and the sa'ibah, and they affirmed it.

Regarding what is meant by ﴿the favour of Allah﴾ there are three opinions:

One: that it is the Tawhid (monotheism). This was said by Ibn Abbas. The second: the Qur'an and the Messenger. The third: the lawful (halal) that Allah made lawful for them.

(p-471) His saying, Exalted: ﴿and they worship besides Allah what has no power to provide for them any sustenance﴾. Regarding what is referred to there are two opinions:

One: that it is the idols, said by Qatadah. The second: the angels, said by Muqatil.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿from the heavens﴾ means the rain, and ﴿from the earth﴾ the plants and fruits.

His saying, Exalted: ﴿anything﴾. Al-Akhfash said: "shay'an" is made a substitute for "rizq," and the meaning is: they do not possess any provision, little or much, ﴿and they are not able﴾, i.e., they are not capable of anything. Al-Farra' said: He said at the beginning "yamliku" (singular) and at the end "yastati'un" (plural), because "ma" in its usage is a collective term for their deities; so He made "yamliku" singular in accordance with the wording of "ma" and its singularity, and made "yastati'un" plural in accordance with the meaning, like His saying: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾ [Yunus: 42].

His saying, Exalted: ﴿So do not strike forth similitudes for Allah﴾, i.e., do not liken Him to His creation, for He resembles nothing and nothing resembles Him. The meaning is: do not make for Him a partner.

Regarding His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah knows, and you do not know﴾ there are four opinions:

The first: He knows the striking of similitudes, and you do not know that. This was said by Ibn al-Sa'ib.

The second: He knows that He has no partner, and you do not know that He has no partner. This was said by Muqatil.

The third: He knows the error of the similitudes you strike, and you do not know the correctness of that from its error.

The fourth: He knows what has been and what will be, and you do not know the measure of His greatness when you associated others with Him and attributed to Him inability to resurrect His creation.

(p. 472) God's words: ﴿God set forth a parable﴾, meaning He presented a likeness through which the intended meaning is made clear. There are two opinions on this:

The first is that it is a parable for the believer and the disbeliever. The one who "has no power over anything" is the disbeliever, because he has no good in him. The one who has provision is the believer, because of the good that is with him. This is the view of Ibn 'Abbas and Qatadah.

The second is that it is a parable God struck for Himself and for the idols, because He is the owner of everything, while they own nothing. This is the view of Mujahid and al-Suddi. It is mentioned in the tafsir (interpretation of the Qur'an) that this parable was struck concerning a people who lived in the time of the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and about them there are two opinions:

The first is that the slave was Abu al-Jiwar, and the one with good provision was his master Hisham ibn 'Amr. This was narrated by 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas. Muqatil said: the slave was Abu al-Hawajir.

The second is that the slave was Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, and the one with good provision was Abu Bakr al-Siddiq, may God be pleased with him. This was said by Ibn Jurayj. As for His words ﴿Are they equal?﴾, He did not say "are they both equal," because the intended meaning is the category. Ibn al-Anbari said: the word "man" (man) is singular in form, but its meaning is plural. The parable was not struck with one specific slave and one specific owner, but it refers to a group of slaves and a group of owners. The scholars said: most of them were described this way, and what is meant is all of them.

God's words: ﴿God set forth a parable: two men, one of them dumb﴾. We have explained "bakam" (dumbness, inability to speak) in Al-Baqarah:18. The meaning of ﴿who has no power over anything﴾ is: of speech, because he cannot understand, nor can he be understood. ﴿And he is a burden upon his master﴾. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, a weight upon his guardian and relatives. Regarding who is meant by this parable there are four opinions:

One: it is a parable God struck for the believer and the disbeliever. The disbeliever is the dumb one, and the one who commands justice is the believer. This was narrated by al-'Awfi from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: it was revealed concerning 'Uthman ibn 'Affan. He is the one who commands justice. The one concerned is a client (mawla) of his who disliked Islam and forbade 'Uthman from spending in the way of God, and he is the dumb one. This was narrated by Ibrahim ibn Ya'la ibn Munyah from Ibn 'Abbas.

The third: it is a parable God struck for Himself and for an idol. The idol is the dumb one, and God is the one who commands justice. This is the view of Mujahid, Qatadah, Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil.

The fourth: the dumb one is Ubayy ibn Khalaf, and the one who commands justice is Hamzah, 'Uthman ibn 'Affan and 'Uthman ibn Maz'un. This was said by 'Ata'.

The first: it is a master in the literal sense, if we say that he is a man among people.

The second: it means "guardian" (waliyy), if we say that he is an idol. The meaning then is: he is a burden upon (p. 474) his guardian, who serves him and adorns him.

If we say he is the idol, then it is because it is inanimate matter. ﴿Is he equal﴾, that is, this dumb one, ﴿with one who commands justice﴾, that is, one who is able to speak and states the truth.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 77:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And to Allah belongs the unseen of the heavens and the earth﴾. We have already mentioned it at the end of (Hud: 123). The occasion of revelation of this verse is that the disbelievers of Makkah asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "When is the Hour?" So this was revealed. This is related by Muqatil. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: The meaning of "the unseen" here is the establishment of the Hour.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And the matter of the Hour is not but as a glance of the eye﴾, meaning: the Resurrection, ﴿or even nearer﴾. Al-lamh (the glance) is looking quickly. The meaning is: the Resurrection, in the swiftness of its establishment and the raising of the creatures, is like the blink of an eye, because Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Be, and it is﴾ [al-Baqarah: 117]. "Or it is nearer." Muqatil said: rather, it is faster. Al-Zajjaj said: It is not meant that the Hour comes in less time than the glance of the eye; rather, it describes the swiftness of the power to bring it about whenever He wills.

(p-٤٧٥)

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And Allah brought you out from the wombs of your mothers﴾. Hamza recited "إمَّهاتِكِمْ" with a kasra on the alif and the mim. Al-Kisa'i recited it with a kasra on the alif and a fatha on the mim. The rest recited it with a damma on the alif and a fatha on the mim. The same applies in (An-Nur: 61), (Az-Zumar: 6) and (An-Najm: 32). There is no disagreement among them about beginning with a damma on the hamza.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And He made for you hearing﴾. Its wording is singular, but what is meant is the plural. We have already explained the reason for this at the beginning of (Al-Baqarah: 7). "Al-af'idah" (the hearts) is the plural of "fu'ad." Al-Zajjaj said: It is like "ghurab" (crow) and "aghribah" (crows). "Fu'ad" was not pluralised in the most common plural pattern, so one does not say "fi'dan," as in "ghurab" and "ghirban."

Abu 'Ubaydah said: He mentioned hearing, sight and hearts before bringing them out, but the Arabs put things first and last. He recited:

Massive, from whom the hanging straps of blood-money are suspended, when the heavy burdens are laid upon him and he bears them.

[Ash-shanaq: what lies between the two obligatory portions.] The "mu'un" (heavy burdens) is greater than the "shanaq," so he began with the lesser before the greater.

The exegetes said: The purpose of the verse is that Allah, Exalted is He, made His blessings clear to them in that He brought them out ignorant of things, and created for them the faculties through which they reach knowledge.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 79:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Subjected in the atmosphere of the sky﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is the air far from the earth.

(p-476) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿None holds them up except Allah﴾. In this there are two opinions:

One of them: none holds them up, when they fold and spread their wings, from falling to the earth except Allah. This is the view of most of the scholars.

The second: none holds them up from sending down stones upon the worst of this nation, as was done to others, except Allah. This is the view of Ibn al-Sa'ib.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 16, verses 80–83:**

Allah's words: ﴿And Allah has made for you, from your houses, a dwelling place﴾, meaning a place in which you dwell. These are the dwellings made of stone and clay, which conceal private parts and women. This is because Allah Most High created the wood, the clay, and the tools with which a house can be built and roofed.

﴿And He has made for you, from the hides of livestock, tents﴾, which are the domed shelters and tents made of leather. ﴿You find them light (tastakhiffunaha)﴾, meaning their carrying is light for you. ﴿On the day of your journey (zaʿnikum)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu ʿAmr read *ẓaʿanikum* with a fatha on the ʿayn. ʿAsim, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read it with a sukun on the ʿayn. Both are dialectal forms, like *al-shaʿar* and *al-shaʿr*, and *al-nahar* and *al-nahr*. The meaning is: when you travel. ﴿And on the day of your settling﴾, meaning they are not burdensome for you in either situation.

﴿And from their wool﴾, meaning sheep; ﴿and their fur﴾, meaning camels; ﴿and their hair﴾, meaning goats; ﴿goods (athath)﴾. Al-Farra' said: *al-athath* means property (*al-mataʿ*), and has no singular, just as *al-mataʿ* has no singular. The Arabs say the plural of *al-mataʿ* is *amtiʿa*. If you pluralized *al-athath*, you would say *thalathat aththa wa uthuth*, like *aʿitha* and *uthuth*, and nothing else. Ibn Qutaybah said: *al-athath* is the household goods, such as bedding and coverings. Abu Zayd said: the singular of *al-athath* is *athatha*. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said *qad atta yaʾutta atta*, meaning he became one who possesses *athath*. It is narrated from al-Khalil that he said: its root meaning is abundance and the gathering of some goods upon others, and from it comes *shaʿar athith*, meaning thick hair.

As for His words ﴿and provision (matāʿan)﴾: it is said that it is mentioned alongside *athath* only because the two words differ.

Regarding His words ﴿for a time (ḥīn)﴾, there are two views:

First: it means death, and the meaning is that they benefit from it until the time of death. This is the view of Ibn ʿAbbas and Mujahid.

Second: it means until the time of decay, so the meaning is until that thing wears out. This is the view of Muqatil.

Allah's words: ﴿And Allah has made for you shade from what He has created﴾, meaning what protects you from the heat of the sun. Regarding this there are five views:

One: it is the shade of clouds, related from Ibn ʿAbbas. Two: the shade of houses, related from Ibn al-Sa'ib. Three: the shade of trees, related from Qatada and al-Zajjaj. Four: the shade of trees and mountains, related from Ibn Qutaybah. Five: it is every thing that has a shade, from a wall, a roof, a tree, a mountain, and other things. This is related from Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi.

Allah's words: ﴿And He has made for you, from the mountains, refuges (aknān)﴾, meaning what shelters you from heat and cold, and these are the caves and tunnels. The singular of *aknān* is *kinn*, and everything that protects something and covers it is a *kinn*.

﴿And He has made for you garments (sarābīl)﴾, which are shirts, ﴿that protect you from the heat﴾. He did not say "cold," because whatever protects from heat also protects from cold. A poet said:

*I do not know, when I set out for a land seeking good, which of the two will come to me first.*

Al-Zajjaj said: He specified heat only because they, in their dwellings, suffered more from heat than from cold. This is the view of ʿAta' al-Khurasani.

Allah's words: ﴿And garments that protect you from your violence (baʾsakum)﴾, meaning the armor with which they protect themselves from the severity of thrusting and striking in battle.

Allah's words: ﴿Thus He completes His favor upon you﴾, meaning just as Allah has bestowed these things upon you, so He completes His favor upon you in this world, ﴿that perhaps you would submit (tuslimūn)﴾. The address is to the people of Makkah, most of whom were disbelievers at that time. If it were said that it addresses the Muslims, the meaning would be: that perhaps you would persist in Islam and uphold its rights. Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, and Abu Raja' read *tuslamūn* with a fatha on the *tāʾ* and the *lām*, meaning: that perhaps when you wear armor, you will be safe (*tuslamūn*) from wounds in battle.

Allah's words: ﴿But if they turn away (tawallaw)﴾, meaning they turn away from faith, ﴿then upon you is only the clear conveyance (al-balāgh al-mubīn)﴾. According to the exegetes, this verse is abrogated (*mansūkha*, meaning its ruling has been replaced by a later ruling) by the verse of the sword.

Allah's words: ﴿They recognize the favor of Allah, then deny it﴾. Regarding this favor there are two views:

First: it refers to the dwellings, which are the favors of Allah Almighty upon them in this world. Regarding their denial of it there are three views. One: they say, "We inherited these from our fathers." Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid who said: The favors of Allah are the dwellings, the livestock, the garments, and the iron. The disbelievers of Quraysh recognize them, then deny them by saying, "These belonged to our fathers, and we inherited them from them." This is from Mujahid. Two: they say, "Were it not for so-and-so, such-and-such would not have happened." This is their denial, related from ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allah. Three: they know that the favors come from Allah, but they say, "These are through the intercession of our gods." This is related from Ibn al-Sa'ib, al-Farra', and Ibn Qutaybah.

Second: the favor here refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). They recognize that he is a prophet, then they deny him. This is related from Mujahid, al-Suddi, and al-Zajjaj.

Allah's words: ﴿And most of them are disbelievers﴾. Al-Hasan said: Indeed all of them are disbelievers, but He mentioned "most" while meaning all.

Allah's words: ﴿And He has made for you, from the mountains, refuges (aknān)﴾, meaning what shelters you from heat and cold, and these are the caves and tunnels. The singular of *aknān* is *kinn*, and everything that protects something and covers it is a *kinn*.

﴿And He has made for you garments (sarābīl)﴾, which are shirts, ﴿that protect you from the heat﴾. He did not say "cold," because whatever protects from heat also protects from cold. A poet said:

*I do not know, when I set out for a land seeking good, which of the two will come to me first.*

Al-Zajjaj said: He specified heat only because they, in their dwellings, suffered more from heat than from cold. This is the view of ʿAta' al-Khurasani.

Allah's words: ﴿And garments that protect you from your violence (baʾsakum)﴾, meaning the armor with which they protect themselves from the severity of thrusting and striking in battle.

Allah's words: ﴿Thus He completes His favor upon you﴾, meaning just as Allah has bestowed these things upon you, so He completes His favor upon you in this world, ﴿that perhaps you would submit (tuslimūn)﴾. The address is to the people of Makkah, most of whom were disbelievers at that time. If it were said that it addresses the Muslims, the meaning would be: that perhaps you would persist in Islam and uphold its rights. Ibn ʿAbbas, Saʿid ibn Jubayr, ʿIkrimah, and Abu Raja' read *tuslamūn* with a fatha on the *tāʾ* and the *lām*, meaning: that perhaps when you wear armor, you will be safe (*tuslamūn*) from wounds in battle.

Allah's words: ﴿But if they turn away (tawallaw)﴾, meaning they turn away from faith, ﴿then upon you is only the clear conveyance (al-balāgh al-mubīn)﴾. According to the exegetes, this verse is abrogated (*mansūkha*, meaning its ruling has been replaced by a later ruling) by the verse of the sword.

Allah's words: ﴿They recognize the favor of Allah, then deny it﴾. Regarding this favor there are two views:

First: it refers to the dwellings, which are the favors of Allah Almighty upon them in this world. Regarding their denial of it there are three views. One: they say, "We inherited these from our fathers." Ibn Abi Najih related from Mujahid who said: The favors of Allah are the dwellings, the livestock, the garments, and the iron. The disbelievers of Quraysh recognize them, then deny them by saying, "These belonged to our fathers, and we inherited them from them." This is from Mujahid. Two: they say, "Were it not for so-and-so, such-and-such would not have happened." This is their denial, related from ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allah. Three: they know that the favors come from Allah, but they say, "These are through the intercession of our gods." This is related from Ibn al-Sa'ib, al-Farra', and Ibn Qutaybah.

Second: the favor here refers to Muhammad (ﷺ). They recognize that he is a prophet, then they deny him. This is related from Mujahid, al-Suddi, and al-Zajjaj.

Allah's words: ﴿And most of them are disbelievers﴾. Al-Hasan said: Indeed all of them are disbelievers, but He mentioned "most" while meaning all.

**Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on Surah 16, verses 80–83:**

Allah's words: ﴿And Allah has made for you, from your houses, a dwelling place﴾, meaning a place in which you dwell. These are the dwellings made of stone and clay, which conceal private parts and women. This is because Allah Most High created the wood, the clay, and the tools with which a house can be built and roofed.

﴿And He has made for you, from the hides of livestock, tents﴾, which are the domed shelters and tents made of leather. ﴿You find them light (tastakhiffunaha)﴾, meaning their carrying is light for you. ﴿On the day of your journey (zaʿnikum)﴾. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', and Abu ʿAmr read *ẓaʿanikum* with a fatha on the ʿayn. ʿAsim, Ibn ʿAmir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read it with a sukun on the ʿayn. Both are dialectal forms, like *al-shaʿar* and *al-shaʿr*, and *al-nahar* and *al-nahr*. The meaning is: when you travel. ﴿And on the day of your settling﴾, meaning they are not burdensome for you in either situation.

﴿And from their wool﴾, meaning sheep; ﴿and their fur﴾, meaning camels; ﴿and their hair﴾, meaning goats; ﴿goods (athath)﴾. Al-Farra' said: *al-athath* means property (*al-mataʿ*), and has no singular, just as *al-mataʿ* has no singular. The Arabs say the plural of *al-mataʿ* is *amtiʿa*. If you pluralized *al-athath*, you would say *thalathat aththa wa uthuth*, like *aʿitha* and *uthuth*, and nothing else. Al-Zajjaj said: it is said *qad atta yaʾutta atta*, meaning he became one who possesses *athath*. It is narrated from al-Khalil that he said: its root meaning is abundance and the gathering of some goods upon others, and from it comes *shaʿar athith*, meaning thick hair.

Second: it means until the time of decay, so the meaning is until that thing wears out. This is the view of Muqatil.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 84–87:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And [mention] the Day when We will raise from every nation a witness﴾. He means the Day of Resurrection, and the witness of each nation is its prophet, who will bear witness against them regarding their affirmation and their denial, ﴿Then permission will not be given to those who disbelieved﴾ to make excuses, ﴿nor will they be asked to make amends﴾. That is, it will not be sought from them that they return to what Allah has commanded, because the Hereafter is not an abode of obligation (taklif).

(p-480) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And when those who did wrong see the punishment﴾, that is, those who associated partners [with Allah], ﴿the punishment﴾, meaning the Fire, ﴿it will not be lightened for them, nor will they be reprieved﴾: they will not be delayed, nor given respite. ﴿And when those who associated partners see their partners﴾, meaning the idols they had made partners with Allah in worship. This is because Allah will raise up every deity other than Him, and the polytheists will say: ﴿Our Lord, these are our partners whom we used to invoke﴾, that is, whom we used to worship besides You.

If it is said: this is already known to Allah, exalted is He, so what is the benefit of their saying: ﴿These are our partners﴾? There are two answers to this:

The first: when they concealed their polytheism in their saying, "By Allah, we were not polytheists," Allah, exalted is He, punished them by sealing their tongues and making their limbs speak. So at the sight of their gods they said: ﴿Our Lord, these are our partners﴾, that is: we have now confessed after denial and affirmed after lying, seeking mercy and fleeing from wrath. This saying of theirs is as an acknowledgment of sin, not as informing One who does not know.

The second: when they witnessed the magnitude of Allah's wrath, they said, "These are our partners," supposing that some relief might come to them from this saying, and that the idols might be held responsible for their crimes or part of their sins, since they had attributed to them reason and discernment. But the idols answered them in a way that cut off their hope.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then they will cast to them the word﴾, that is: the idols answered them and said to them, ﴿Indeed, you are liars.﴾ Al-Farra' said: "Their gods returned their saying to them." Abu 'Ubayda said: "﴿fa-alqaw﴾" means "they said to them." It is said: "I cast to so-and-so such-and-such," meaning "I said to him." The scholars said: they denied them in their worship of them, because the idols were inanimate and did not know their worshippers. Their disgrace became evident on that Day when they had worshipped one who did not know of their worship, and this is like His saying: ﴿They will deny their worship of them﴾ [Maryam 19:82].

(p-481) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will offer submission to Allah on that Day﴾. The meaning: they will submit to Him. Regarding those referred to there are two views:

The first: they are the polytheists; this is what most of the scholars said. Then regarding the meaning of their submission there are two views: one, that they submitted [to Him] by acknowledging His oneness and lordship; the other, that they submitted to His punishment.

The second: they are the polytheists and the idols all together. Al-Kalbi said: the meaning is that they submitted to Allah, yielding to His judgment.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what they used to invent will be lost to them﴾. Regarding this there are two views: one, that their claim that the idols would intercede for them has been nullified; the other, that what Satan had adorned for them, namely that Allah has a partner and a son, has gone from them.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 88–89:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Those who disbelieve and bar [others] from the way of Allah﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: They prevented people from obeying Allah and from believing in Muhammad (ﷺ).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿We will increase them in punishment upon punishment﴾. He made the first punishment indefinite (nakkara al-'adhab) because it is a specific kind for a particular people, and He made the second punishment definite (ʿarrafa al-ʿadhab) because it is the punishment with which most of the people of the Fire are punished, so in its fame it held the same status as "the Fire" in the saying of one who says: "We seek refuge in Allah from the Fire." It has also been said: this punishment was added to what they deserve of their punishment, because of their barring others from the way of Allah.

Regarding the description of this punishment with which they were increased, there are four opinions:

The first: that it is scorpions like tall palm trees. This was narrated by Masruq from Ibn Mas'ud.

The second: that it is serpents like elephants and scorpions like mules. This was narrated by Zirr from Ibn Mas'ud.

The third: that it is five rivers of molten brass flowing from beneath the Throne, with which they are punished: three according to the length of the night and two according to the length of the day. This was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The fourth: that it is the zamharir (extreme cold), mentioned by Ibn al-Anbari.

Al-Zajjaj said: They will pass from the heat of the Fire to the zamharir, and then they will rush from its intense cold back to the Fire.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And We have brought you as a witness over these﴾. Regarding those referred to, there are two opinions:

The first: that they are his people; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas.

The second: that they are his community (ummah); this was said by Muqatil. Here the statement is complete. Then He said: ﴿And We have sent down to you the Book as an explanation (tibyanan)﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: tibyan is a noun carrying the meaning of bayan (clarification).

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿for every thing﴾, the scholars of meanings (ʿulama' al-maʿani) said: [it means] for every matter of the religion, either by explicit statement concerning it, or by referral to that which necessitates knowledge, such as the clarification of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) or the consensus (ijma') of the Muslims.

Regarding al-munkar (the reprehensible), there are four opinions:

The first: it is polytheism (al-shirk). Muqatil said it. The second: it is what is not recognised in the sharia or the sunnah. The third: it is what Allah has promised the Fire for. Ibn al-Sa'ib mentioned these two. The fourth: that a person's outward appearance is better than his inner state. Sufyan ibn 'Uyaynah said it.

As for al-baghy (oppression), Ibn 'Abbas said: it is injustice (al-zulm). Its explanation has already passed in several places [al-Baqarah: 173; al-A'raf: 33; Yunus: 23, 90].

Regarding His saying, ﴿He admonishes you﴾, Ibn 'Abbas said: "He disciplines you." We have already mentioned the meaning of admonition (al-wa'z) in (Surat al-Nisa': 58). And ﴿you may remember﴾ means: "you may be mindful" (tatta'izun). Ibn Mas'ud said: "This is the most comprehensive verse in the Qur'an for good or for evil." al-Hasan said: "By Allah, justice and excellence have left out no act of obedience to [Allah] without encompassing it, and indecency, the reprehensible and oppression have left out no act of disobedience to Allah without including it."

Regarding His saying, ﴿And fulfil the covenant of Allah﴾, they differed about who it was revealed concerning, in two opinions:

One: it was revealed concerning the alliances of the people of the Jahiliyyah (pre-Islamic era). Mujahid and Qatadah said it. The second: it was revealed concerning those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ. The exegetes said: the covenant that must be fulfilled is that whose performance is good; when a servant makes a covenant concerning it, fulfilling it becomes obligatory, and a promise is among the covenants. ﴿And do not break oaths after their confirmation﴾, i.e., after their strengthening and solidifying with resolve and binding oneself by the oath, unlike the idle oath (laghw al-yamin). "Wakkadtu al-shay'a tawkidan" is the dialect of the people of the Hijaz. As for the people of Najd, they say: "akkadtuhu ta'kidan." al-Zajjaj said: "It is said: wakkadtu al-amr and akkadtu are two good dialectal forms; the original is the waw, and the hamza is a substitute for it."

[p. 484]

Regarding His saying, ﴿And you have made Allah your surety over you﴾, i.e., for fulfilling it. That is because whoever swears by Allah has, as it were, made Allah a guarantor of fulfilling what he swore to.

The exegetes have three opinions regarding the meaning of "kafila" (surety):

The first: a witness (shahid). Sa'id ibn Jubayr said it. The second: a trustee (wakil). Mujahid said it. The third: a guardian, watching over your covenant. Abu Sulayman al-Dimashqi said it.

Regarding His saying, ﴿And do not be like the one who unravels her yarn﴾, Mujahid said: "This is the act of the women of the people of Najd: one of them unravels her rope, then teases it out, then mixes it with wool and spins it." Muqatil said: "She is a woman from Quraysh called 'Rayta' daughter of 'Amr ibn Ka'b; whenever she spun, she would unravel it." Ibn al-Sa'ib said: her name is "Ra'ita." Ibn al-Anbari said: her name is "Rayta" daughter of 'Amr al-Marriyya, and her epithet is al-Ja'ra', and she was from the people of Makkah, and she was well known among the addressees, so they recognised her by her description, and there was no parallel to her in that act. She was extremely foolish: she would spin thread from cotton or wool and make it firm, then order her slave-girl to cut it up. Some said: she and her slave-girls would spin, then she would order them to unravel what they had spun, so Allah struck her as a parable for those who break covenants. "Naqadat" here means "tanqudu" (unravels), as in His saying: ﴿And the companions of the Garden will call out﴾ [al-A'raf: 43], meaning "and will call out."

Regarding what is meant by "ghazl" (spinning), there are two opinions:

One: it is well-known spinning, whether of cotton, wool or hair. This is the view of the majority. The second: it is the rope (habl). Mujahid said it.

As for His saying, ﴿after strength﴾, Qatadah said: "after tightening (ibram)." And His saying, ﴿into pieces (ankathan)﴾, i.e., unravelled. Ibn Qutaybah said: "al-ankath are what has been unravelled of spun hair or other material; its singular is nikth." The meaning is: do not confirm your oaths and covenants among yourselves and then undo them and break them, so that you would be like a woman who spun and wove, then unravelled that weave and made it into pieces.

[p. 485]

Regarding His saying, ﴿You take your oaths as deception between you﴾, i.e., corruption (daghal), deceit, and trickery. Every thing into which a defect has entered is "madkhul," and there is "dakhal" in it.

Regarding His saying, ﴿lest one community be more numerous﴾, Ibn Qutaybah said: "li-an takuna ummatun" (in order that a community may be), ﴿is more than (arba)﴾, i.e., richer than ﴿another community﴾. al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is: "that a community be more numerous." It is said: "raba al-shay'u yarbu" when it increases. Ibn al-Anbari said: the linguists said: "arba" means greater in number. Mujahid said: "They used to make alliances with allies, and they would find among them more people and more honour, so they would break the alliance with these and make alliance with those, so they were forbidden from that." al-Farra' said: the meaning is: do not betray a people because of their small number and your large number, or your small number and their large number, when you have deceived them with oaths.

Regarding His saying, ﴿Allah only tests you by it﴾, there are three opinions concerning this verse:

One: it refers to the abundance (al-kathrah). Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Ibn al-Sa'ib and Muqatil said it. The meaning is: Allah only tests you by abundance. If there is a covenant between two groups and one of them is more numerous, one should not dissolve the covenant between oneself and the smaller group. If it is said: when He referred to abundance by a pronoun, why was it not said "bihi" (in it, masculine)? Ibn al-Anbari answered that: the feminine of "kathrah" is not a real feminine, so it was treated according to the sense of the masculine, just as "al-sayha" (the cry) is treated according to the sense of "al-siyah" (the shouting).

The second: it refers to the covenant, since the oaths indicate it, so it functions as if it were explicitly mentioned. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned it.

The third: it refers to the command to fulfil (the covenant). Some exegetes mentioned it.

Regarding His saying, ﴿And if Allah had willed, He would have made you one community﴾, we have already explained it at the end of (Surat Hud: 118).

[p. 487]

Regarding His saying, ﴿but He leaves astray whom He wills﴾, it is explicit in refuting the Qadariyya (those who deny divine decree), since He attributed misguidance and guidance to Himself and made them contingent upon His will.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 94–96:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And do not take your oaths as means of deceit among yourselves, lest a foot slip after being firm﴾. This is a resumption of the prohibition against oaths of deception. ﴿Lest a foot slip after being firm﴾. Abu 'Ubayda said: This is a proverb said of every person afflicted after well-being, or who falls into a predicament after safety: "His foot slipped." Muqatil said: The one who breaks the covenant slips in his religion as a man's foot slips after being steady. The commentators said: This is a prohibition addressed to those who pledged allegiance to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) to Islam and to supporting the religion, against breaking the covenant. What supports this is His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And you would taste the evil﴾, meaning: the punishment, ﴿for what you hindered from the way of Allah﴾. He means that when they broke their covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), they barred people from Islam, and so they deserved the punishment.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And for you is a great punishment﴾, meaning: in the Hereafter. Then He emphasized this with His saying: ﴿And do not exchange the covenant of Allah for a small price﴾. Abu Salih related from Ibn 'Abbas: It was revealed concerning "two men who disputed before the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) over a piece of land. One of them was called 'Idan ibn Ash'a', who was the owner of the land, and the other was 'Imru' al-Qays, who was the defendant. 'Imru' al-Qays intended to swear an oath, so the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) delayed him, and this verse was revealed." Abu Bakr al-Khatib mentioned that the name of the owner of the land was "Rabi'a ibn 'Idan," and it was said: "'Iyadan," with a fatha on the ʿayn and a dotted yāʾ with two dots below. The meaning of the verse: Do not break your covenants, seeking by breaking them a small share of the worldly life. Indeed, what is with Allah of reward for fulfilling is better for you than what is immediate. ﴿What is with you will end﴾, i.e., will perish, ﴿and what is with Allah﴾ in the Hereafter ﴿is lasting﴾. Ibn Kathir stopped on the yāʾ in one narration from him, and there is no disagreement about its deletion in continuous recitation. ﴿And We will surely reward those who were patient﴾. Nafi', Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, Hamza, and al-Kisa'i read "wa-la-yajziyanna" with a yāʾ. Ibn Kathir and ʿĀṣim read "wa-lanajziyanna" with a nūn. They did not differ regarding "wa-lanajziyannahum ajrahum" that it is with a nūn. The meaning of this verse: And those who were patient in obeying His command will surely be recompensed with the best of what they used to do in the world, and He will overlook their misdeeds.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 97:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whoever does righteousness, whether male or female, while being a believer﴾. Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts. The first: that Imru' al-Qays, mentioned earlier, acknowledged the truth which he had intended to swear falsely about, and so this verse was revealed concerning him: ﴿Whoever does righteousness﴾, which is his acknowledgment of the truth. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: that some people from among the People of the Torah, the People of the Gospel, and the People of Idols sat together and boasted over one another, and so this verse was revealed. This was related by Abu Salih.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿We will surely give them a good life﴾. The scholars differed as to where this good life will be, and there are three opinions:

The first: that it is in this world. This was narrated by al-Awfi from Ibn Abbas. Then, concerning it, the exegetes have nine opinions. The first: that it is contentment (qana'ah), said by Ali, peace be upon him, Ibn Abbas in one narration, al-Hasan in one narration, and Wahb ibn Munabbih. The second: that it is lawful provision, narrated by Abu Malik from Ibn Abbas. Al-Dahhak said: he eats what is lawful and wears what is lawful. The third: that it is happiness, narrated by Ali ibn Abi Talhah from Ibn Abbas. The fourth: that it is obedience, said by Ikrimah. The fifth: that it is provision day by day, said by Qatadah. The sixth: that it is good provision and righteous deed, said by Isma'il ibn Abi Khalid. The seventh: that it is the sweetness of obedience, said by Abu Bakr al-Warraq. The eighth: well-being and sufficiency. The ninth: contentment with the decree, both of these mentioned by al-Mawardi.

The second: that it is in the Hereafter, said by al-Hasan, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, Qatadah, and Ibn Zayd, and that only happens in Paradise.

The third: that it is in the grave, narrated by Abu Ghassan from Sharik.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 98–102:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So when you recite the Qur'an, seek refuge in Allah﴾. There are three opinions concerning this:

One: The meaning is: when you intend to recite, then seek refuge. Similar to it is ﴿O you who believe, when you rise to prayer, wash your faces﴾ [al-Ma'idah 5:6], and His saying: ﴿And when you ask them for any article, ask them from behind a screen﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:53], and His saying: ﴿When you consult the Messenger, present a charity before your consultation﴾ [al-Mujadilah 58:12].

Similar to it in speech: "When you eat, say: In the name of Allah." This is the view of the majority of scholars and the linguists (lughawiyyun).

Two: It is to be taken literally, and seeking refuge is after the recitation. This was narrated from Abu Hurayrah and Dawud (al-Zahiri).

Three: It is of the inverted order (al-muqaddam wa'l-mu'akhkhar), so the meaning is: when you have sought refuge in Allah, then recite. This was stated by Abu Hatim al-Sijistani. The first is the most sound.

Section

Seeking refuge when reciting is a sunnah in prayer and outside it.

Concerning its wording, there are two narrations from Ahmad:

One: "I seek refuge in Allah from the accursed Satan; indeed Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing." Narrated by Abu Bakr al-Marwazi.

The second: "I seek refuge in Allah, the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing, from the accursed Satan; indeed Allah is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing." Narrated by Hanbal. We have explained the meaning of "a'udhu" (I seek refuge) at the beginning of the book [p. 7], and explained the derivation of "Satan" (al-shaytan) at (al-Baqarah 2:14), and "accursed" (al-rajim) at (Al 'Imran 3:36).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, he has no authority over those who believe﴾. Regarding the meaning of "authority" (sultan) there are two opinions:

One: It is domination (al-taslut). Concerning this there are three opinions: First: He has no authority over them at all, because Allah has turned away his authority from them by His saying: ﴿Indeed, My servants, you have no authority over them, except those who follow you of the deviators﴾ [al-Hijr 15:42]. Second: He has no authority over them, because of their seeking refuge from him. Third: He has no capacity to bring them to a sin that is not forgiven.

Two: It is proof (al-hujjah). The meaning is: he has no proof for what he calls them to of disobedience. This was stated by Mujahid.

(p-491) As for His saying "yatawallawnahu" (they take him as ally), its meaning is: they obey him.

Concerning the pronoun in His saying: ﴿And those who associate others with Him﴾ (wa'lladhina hum bihi mushrikun), there are two opinions:

One: It refers to Allah, the Exalted. This was stated by Mujahid and al-Dahhak.

Two: It refers to Satan, so the meaning is: those who, because of him, are associators with Allah. This is like one saying: "So-and-so became knowledgeable through you," meaning: because of you. This is the statement of Ibn Qutaybah. Ibn al-Anbari said: the meaning is: those who, by their associating Iblis (Satan) in worship, are associators with Allah, Exalted is He.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And when We substitute one verse in place of another verse﴾. The occasion of its revelation was that Allah, Exalted is He, would send down a verse, it would be acted upon for a period, then He would abrogate it. The disbelievers of Quraysh said: "By Allah, Muhammad only mocks his companions: he commands them today with one matter, and comes to them tomorrow with what is easier for them than it." So this verse was revealed. This was stated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The meaning: when We abrogate a verse with another verse, whether the abrogation of the ruling and the recitation, or the abrogation of the ruling while the recitation remains. ﴿And Allah knows best what He sends down﴾ of abrogating and abrogated, and of severity and leniency; He knows the benefit in that. ﴿They say, "You are only a fabricator"﴾, that is: a liar. ﴿But most of them do not know﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions: One: they do not know that Allah sent it down. Two: they do not know the wisdom of abrogation.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: The Holy Spirit has brought it down﴾, meaning: the Qur'an; ﴿the Holy Spirit﴾ meaning Jibril (Gabriel). We have explained this name at (al-Baqarah 2:87).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿from your Lord﴾, that is: from His speech; ﴿with truth﴾, that is: with the correct matter; ﴿to make firm those who believe﴾ by what it contains of clear proofs, so that they increase in certainty.

As for the first reading, Ibn Qutaybah said: "yulhidoona" means they incline towards him and claim that he teaches him; the origin of *ilhad* is inclination. Al-Farra' said: "yulhidoona" with a damma on the ya' means they raise objections (ya'taridoon), and from it is His saying: ﴿And whoever intends therein deviation by wrongdoing﴾ [al-Hajj 22:25], that is, by objection. And "yalhadoona" with a fatha on the ya' means they incline. Al-Zajjaj said: *yulhidoona ilayhi* means they incline the statement concerning it, that it is non-Arabic.

Ibn Qutaybah said: The common people hardly distinguish between *ajami* and *a'jami*, or between *'arabi* and *a'rabi*. The *a'jami* is one who does not speak clearly, even if he dwells in the desert; the *ajami* is one ascribed to the non-Arabs even if he is eloquent; the *a'rabi* is the Bedouin; and the *'arabi* is one ascribed to the Arabs even if he is not a Bedouin.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And this is a tongue﴾, meaning: the Qur'an, ﴿clear ('arabiyy)﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: That is, its bearer speaks in Arabic.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Only those who do not believe in the signs of Allah fabricate lies﴾, that is: those who, when they see the signs which none but Allah can produce, deny them. ﴿And those are the liars﴾, that is: lying is an inseparable description of them and one of their habits. This is a rebuttal of them when they said: ﴿You are only a fabricator﴾ [al-Nahl 16:101]. This verse is among the most eloquent warnings against lying, because it is specified for those who do not believe.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 106–111:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Whoever disbelieves in Allah after his belief﴾. Muqatil said: It was revealed concerning ʿAbdullah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh al-Qurashi, Miqyas ibn Subabah, ʿAbdullah ibn Unays ibn Khatal, Tuʿmah ibn Ubayriq, Qays ibn al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah, and Qays ibn al-Faki al-Makhzumi.

So there was revealed: ﴿except one who is forced [to it] while his heart is secure in faith﴾. ʿIkrimah related it from Ibn ʿAbbas, and Mujahid said likewise.

Section

Compulsion to the word of disbelief permits uttering it.

Regarding the compulsion that permits this, there are two narrations from Ahmad:

One: that he fears for his own self or for some of his limbs destruction if he does not do what he was commanded.

The second: that intimidation does not constitute compulsion unless it is inflicted through punishment. Since the permissibility of taqiyyah (dissimulation for protection) is established, the better course is not to do it, as Ahmad stated explicitly, regarding a captive who was given the choice between being killed and drinking wine. He said: if he endures being killed, he has honour, and if he does not endure, he has the concession. The apparent meaning of this is permissibility. Al-Athram related from him that he was asked about taqiyyah in drinking wine and said: taqiyyah is only in speech. The apparent meaning of this is that it is not permissible for him to do that. As for when he is compelled to fornication, it is not permissible for him to do the act, and his compulsion is not valid, as Ahmad stated explicitly. If he is compelled to divorce, his divorce does not take effect, as Ahmad stated explicitly, and this is the view of Malik and al-Shafiʿi. Abu Hanifah said it takes effect.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿That is because they preferred the worldly life over the Hereafter﴾. Regarding what is indicated by "that," there are two opinions:

One: it is the wrath and the punishment, said by Muqatil.

The second: it is the opening of the breast to disbelief. And "preferred" means: they loved the world and chose it over the Hereafter.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and that Allah﴾, meaning: and because Allah does not will to guide them. What follows has already been explained [2:7, 4:155, 5:67], up to His saying: ﴿and it is they who are the heedless﴾. There are two opinions concerning it:

One: the heedless of what is intended for them, said by Ibn ʿAbbas. The second: heedless of the Hereafter, said by Muqatil.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Undoubtedly﴾. We have explained it at (Hud: 22).

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, for those who emigrated after they were tried﴾. They differed concerning whom it was revealed, in four opinions:

The first: that it was revealed concerning those among the Companions of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ who were being tried in Mecca. Saʿid ibn Jubayr related it from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The second: that a group of Muslims set out for emigration, and the polytheists overtook them and yielded them to the trial, so there was revealed concerning them: ﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah," but when he is harmed for the sake of Allah, he regards the trial of people as the punishment of Allah﴾ [29:10]. The Muslims wrote to them about that, so they went out, and the polytheists overtook them and fought them, until whoever was saved was saved, and whoever was killed was killed. So this verse was revealed concerning them. ʿIkrimah related it from Ibn ʿAbbas.

The third: that it was revealed concerning ʿAbdullah ibn Saʿd ibn Abi Sarh, whom Satan had caused to slip until he joined the disbelievers. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ ordered that he be killed on the day of the conquest, but ʿUthman ibn ʿAffan sought protection for him, and the Messenger of Allah ﷺ granted him protection. This is narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, al-Hasan, and ʿIkrimah. But it is distant, because the one referred to, although he returned to Islam, the emigration ended with the conquest.

The fourth: that it was revealed concerning ʿAyyash ibn Abi Rabiʿah, Abu Jandal ibn Suhayl ibn ʿAmr, and ʿAbdullah ibn Usayd al-Thaqafi. This was said by Muqatil.

As for His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿after they were tried﴾, most readers recited "futinu" with a damma on the fa' and a kasra on the ta', meaning: after the polytheists tried them away from their religion. Ibn ʿAbbas said: futinu means ʿudhdhibu (they were punished). ʿAbdullah ibn ʿAmir recited "fatanu" with a fatha on the fa' and the ta', meaning: after they tried the people away from the religion of Allah, referring to those among the polytheists who had become Muslim. Abu ʿAli said: after they tried themselves by showing what they showed for dissimulation, because the concession had not yet been revealed.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then they struggled﴾, meaning: they fought alongside the Messenger of Allah ﷺ, ﴿and were patient﴾ in the religion and in jihad. ﴿Indeed, your Lord, after it﴾: regarding the referent of "it," there are four opinions:

One: the trial, which is the view of Muqatil. The second: the deed they committed, said by al-Zajjaj. The third: the striving, the emigration, and the patience. The fourth: the emigration. Ibn al-Anbari mentioned these two and the two preceding them.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿on the Day when every soul will come pleading for itself﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative under one of two possibilities: either the meaning is "indeed your Lord is Forgiving on the day when...," or the meaning is "remember the day when..." The meaning of ﴿pleading for itself﴾ is: pleading on its own behalf. The intended sense is that every person pleads for himself. It has been related from ʿUmar ibn al-Khattab that he said to Kaʿb al-Ahbar: "O Kaʿb, frighten us." And the confirmation of this in the Book of Allah is: ﴿on the Day when every soul will come pleading for itself﴾. We have explained the meaning of pleading at (Hud: 32).

Then Allah sent upon them hunger, until they were eating what they sat upon. This was said by al-Hasan (al-Basri). As for what is narrated from Hafsah (may Allah be pleased with her) that she said: "It is Madinah," that is by way of illustration (tamthil), not as an exegesis (tafsir). Its clarification is what Sulaym ibn 'Anz narrated, who said: "We returned from the Hajj with Hafsah, while 'Uthman was besieged in Madinah. She saw two riders and asked them about him. They said: 'He has been killed.' She said: 'By the One in whose hand is my soul, it is indeed the town,' meaning the Madinah of which Allah, Exalted is He, said in His Book: ﴿And Allah presents an example: a town that was secure and tranquil﴾." Hafsah meant that it was upright in its conduct during the days of the Prophet (ﷺ), Abu Bakr and 'Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both), ﴿but it denied the favours of Allah﴾ at the killing of 'Uthman (may Allah be pleased with him). The meaning of ﴿secure﴾ is: possessing security, in which its people feel safe from being raided. "Tranquil" means: settled, its inhabitants not needing to move away from it out of fear or hardship. We have already explained the meaning of "ample provision" (raghad) in (al-Baqarah: 35, 58).

His saying: ﴿from every place﴾, meaning: there is brought to it from every land. All of this was by the supplication of Ibrahim (peace be upon him). ﴿But it denied the favours of Allah﴾ by their denial of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ).

Regarding the singular of "al-an'um" (favours) there are two opinions:

One: that its singular is "nu'm." This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah and Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: its singular is "ni'mah." This was said by al-Zajjaj. Ibn Qutaybah said: "The view of the one who says it is the plural of 'ni'mah' is not correct, because the pattern "fi'lah" is not pluralised into "af'ul." Rather, it is the plural of "nu'm," as one says: "yawm nu'm" (a pleasant day) and "yawm bu's" (a day of hardship), and it is pluralised as "an'aman" and "ab'usan."

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So Allah made them taste the garment of hunger and fear﴾. 'Ubayd ibn 'Aqil and 'Abd al-Warith narrated from Abu 'Amr: "wa-l-khawf" with a fatha on the fa'. The original sense of "dhawq" (tasting) is with the mouth, and this is a metaphorical usage of it. We have explained this meaning in (Al 'Imran: 106, 185). The word "garment" (libas) is mentioned here figuratively, because of the visible effect of hunger and fear upon them, and it is like His saying: ﴿and the garment of piety﴾ [al-A'raf: 26], for the visible effect of piety upon the God-conscious person. The exegetes said: Allah punished them with hunger for seven years, until they ate carrion and burnt bones. As for fear, it was their fear of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and of his expeditions which he would send around them. The discourse in this verse is directed at the town, while what is meant is its people; for this reason He said: ﴿because of what they used to do﴾, meaning: because of their denial of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), their expulsion of him, and what they plotted of killing him.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 113:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And there had certainly come to them a messenger from among themselves﴾, meaning the people of Makkah, [one who was] "a messenger from among them", meaning Muhammad (ﷺ). ﴿But they denied him, so the punishment seized them﴾. Concerning this there are two opinions:

One of them: that it is hunger; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: the killing at Badr; this was said by Mujahid. Ibn al-Sa'ib said: ﴿while they were wrongdoers﴾, meaning: disbelievers.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 114–115:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾. Regarding who is being addressed by this, there are two opinions:

One of them: they are the Muslims, and this is the saying of the majority (jumhur).

The second: they are the polytheists of Makkah. When their hunger became severe, their leaders spoke to the Messenger of Allah ﷺ and said: "If you have been hostile to the men, what is the matter with the women and the children?" So the Messenger of Allah ﷺ permitted the people to carry food to them. This was related by al-Tha'labi, and al-Farra' mentioned something similar. This verse and the one that follows it are explained in (al-Baqarah 2:172–173).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 114–115:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So eat of what Allah has provided for you﴾. Regarding who is being addressed by this, there are two opinions:

(p-502) His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And do not say, concerning what your tongues describe falsely⁠—﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: the lam in "li-ma" (لِما) has the meaning of "because of" (min ajli). The summary of the statement is: "Do not say, 'This carrion is lawful, and this baḥīrah is unlawful,' because of your lying and your presumption in describing and conjecturing about what has no basis." Here the lam operates in the same manner as in His saying: ﴿And indeed, he is intensely devoted to wealth﴾ [al-ʿĀdiyāt 100:8], meaning: "And indeed he is stingy because of his love of wealth." The word "ma" (ما) has the meaning of a verbal noun (maṣdar), and "al-kadhib" (الكَذِبَ) is in the accusative governed by "tasif" (تَصِفُ). The summary is: "Do not say, due to the description your tongues make of the lie." Ibn Abi ʿAblah read "al-kudhub" (الكُذُبَ). Ibn al-Qasim said: it is an adjective describing the tongues, and it is the plural of "kadhub" (كَذُوب, one who lies habitually). The exegetes said: the meaning is that your declaring lawful and unlawful has no meaning other than lying. The reference in His saying ﴿This is lawful and this is unlawful﴾ is to what they used to make lawful and unlawful, ﴿so that you may fabricate against Allah the lie﴾. That is because they would attribute that declaring lawful and unlawful to Allah, may He be exalted, saying, "He commanded us with this."

His saying: ﴿A brief enjoyment⁠—﴾ means: their enjoyment from what they did is brief.

**Ibn al-Jawzi, *Zad al-Masir*, on Surah 16, verses 118–119:**

Allah's saying: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade what We have related to you before,﴾ He means by this (p. 503) what was mentioned in (al-An'am: 126), which is His saying: ﴿And to those who were Jews We forbade every animal with claws,﴾ ﴿And We did not wrong them﴾ by Our forbidding them what We forbade, ﴿but they were wronging themselves﴾ through rebellion and disobedience.

Allah's saying: ﴿Then indeed your Lord, toward those who did evil in ignorance,﴾ we have explained this in Surah (al-Nisa': 17). We explained repentance (tawbah) and reform (islah) in (al-Baqarah: 160), and we mentioned the meaning of His saying ﴿after it﴾ earlier.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verses 120–122:

Allah's words: ﴿Indeed, Abraham was a nation﴾. Ibn al-Anbari said: This is like the saying of the Arabs: "So-and-so is a mercy (rahmah)," "So-and-so is a knowledge-bearer ('allamah)," and "a genealogist (nassabah)." By this feminine form they intend the extreme degree of the meaning they describe. The Arabs also apply indefinite nouns to a group and to an individual, as in His words: ﴿Then the angels called to him﴾ [Al 'Imran: 39], though it was Gabriel alone who called to him.

The exegetes have three opinions regarding the meaning of "nation" (ummah) here:

The first: that the ummah is one who teaches good. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud, al-Farra' and Ibn Qutaybah.

The second: that he was the only believer in his time. This meaning was transmitted by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas, and Mujahid also said it.

The third: that he was the imam who is followed. This was said by Qatadah, Muqatil and Abu 'Ubaydah, and it has the same meaning as the first opinion. As for "devoutly obedient" (qanit), Ibn Mas'ud said: it means obedient (al-muti'). We have explained "qunut" in (al-Baqarah: 116, 238), and likewise "hanif" [al-Baqarah: 135].

(p-504) Allah's words: ﴿And he was not﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: its original form is lam yakun, and the nun was elided according to Sibawayh because this particle is used very frequently. The leading Basran grammarians mentioned that it could bear elision only because it combines frequent use, that it expresses everything that has passed of actions and everything that is yet to come, that it resembles the letters of softness (huruf al-lin), that it can serve as a sign just as the letters of softness serve as signs, and that it is a nasal sound issuing from the nose; for this reason it admits elision.

Allah's words: ﴿Thankful for His favors﴾. It is in the accusative as a substitute (badal) for His words: ﴿a nation, devoutly obedient﴾. We have already mentioned the singular of "an'um" (favors) a moment ago, and we explained the meaning of "ijtiba'" (choosing) in (al-An'am: 87). Muqatil said: what is meant by "the straight path" here is Islam.

Allah's words: ﴿And We gave him in this world good﴾. Regarding it there are six opinions:

The first: that it is good remembrance; this was said by Ibn 'Abbas. The second: prophethood; this was said by al-Hasan.

The third: a tongue of truthfulness (lisan sidq); this was said by Mujahid. The fourth: the agreement of the religious communities upon his guardianship, so that all of them take him as their ally and are pleased with him; this was said by Qatadah. The fifth: that it is blessing upon him coupled with blessing upon Muhammad (ﷺ); this was said by Muqatil ibn Hayyan. The sixth: righteous children in old age; this was related by al-Tha'labi. The rest of the verse is explained in (al-Baqarah: 130).

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 123:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Then We revealed to you, [O Muhammad], that you follow the religion of Abraham, inclining toward truth﴾. "Millah" (religion, community of faith) means his dīn (religion).

Concerning what he was commanded to follow of that, there are two views:

One of them: he was commanded to follow him in all of his millah, except what he was commanded to abandon. This is the apparent meaning.

[The second: following him in disavowing the idols and adhering to religion through Islam, as said by (p-505) Abu Ja'far al-Tabari.]

In this verse there is evidence for the permissibility of following one who is less excellent (al-mafdul), because our Messenger is the most excellent of the messengers, and he was only commanded to follow him (Abraham) for his precedence in speaking the truth.

Commentary of Ibn al-Jawzi (Zad al-Masir) on surah 16, verse 124:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, the Sabbath was only made﴾ means: it was only enjoined to honour it and to forbid work on it. Al-Hasan and Abu Haywa recited: ﴿innama judila﴾ with a fatha on the jim and the ayn, and ﴿as-sabt﴾ with a fatha on the ta', ﴿upon those who differed concerning it﴾, and the pronoun (in "fihi," "concerning it") refers to the Sabbath.

Regarding the meaning of their disagreement concerning it, there are two opinions:

The first: Musa (Moses) said to them, "Devote yourselves to Allah one day out of every seven days, and worship Him on the day of Friday, and do not do any of your work on it." They refused to accept this and said, "We only want the day on which creation was completed, and that is the day of Saturday." So this was imposed upon them, and it was made strict for them in respect of it. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas. Muqatil said: When Musa commanded them concerning the day of Friday, they said, "We will devote ourselves on the day of Saturday, for Allah did not create anything in it." He said, "I was only commanded concerning the day of Friday." Their rabbis said, "Abide by the command of your Prophet," but they refused. That is their disagreement. When Musa saw their eagerness for the Sabbath, he commanded them regarding it, and they then made sinful acts lawful for themselves on it. Sa'id ibn Jubayr related from Ibn Abbas that he said: Musa saw a man carrying reeds on the Sabbath, so he struck his neck, and birds gathered over him for forty mornings. Ibn Qutayba mentioned in "Mukhtalif al-Hadith": "Allah, the Exalted, sent Musa with the Sabbath, and the Sabbath was abrogated by (the coming of) the Messiah."

The second: some of them made it lawful, and some of them made it forbidden; this was said by Qatada.

(p-506) His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord﴾. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was revealed together with the verse that follows it, and we will mention the occasion of revelation there. As for "the way" (al-sabil), Muqatil said: it is the religion of Islam.

Regarding what is meant by "wisdom" (al-hikmah) there are three opinions:

The first: it is the Qur'an, narrated by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it is jurisprudence (al-fiqh), said by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: it is prophethood, mentioned by al-Zajjaj.

Regarding "the good admonition" (al-maw'izah al-hasanah) there are two opinions:

One: it is the admonitions of the Qur'an, said by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas. The second: it is the fine manners that they recognize, said by al-Dahhak from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And argue with them﴾. Regarding whom this refers to there are two opinions:

One: they are the people of Makkah, said by Abu Salih. The second: they are the People of the Book, said by Muqatil.

Regarding His saying: ﴿in the way that is best﴾ there are three opinions:

The first: argue with them by means of the Qur'an. The second: by "There is no god but Allah"; both opinions were related from Ibn 'Abbas. The third: argue with them without harshness or roughness, and lower your side to them, said by al-Zajjaj. Some scholars of tafsir said: this is abrogated by the verse of the sword.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is most knowing﴾. The meaning: He is most knowing of the two groups, so He commands you regarding them with what is good.

(p-507) **His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And if you retaliate, then retaliate with the like of what you were made to suffer﴾.** Concerning the occasion of its revelation there are two accounts.

The first: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) stood over Hamza, saw him slain, and nothing pained his heart more than that. He said: 'By Allah, I will mutilate seventy of them.' Then Jibril descended while the Prophet (ﷺ) was standing, with the words: ﴿And if you retaliate﴾ . . . to the end of it. So the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was patient and expiated his oath." This was related by Abu Hurayra. Ibn Abbas said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) saw Hamza with his belly ripped open and his ears cut off, and he said: 'Were it not that women would grieve, or that it would become a sunnah after me, I would leave him until Allah raises him from the bellies of beasts and birds. And I will kill seventy men of them in his place.' Then there descended His saying: ﴿Invite to the way of your Lord﴾ up to His saying: ﴿And your patience is not except by Allah﴾." Al-Dahhak related from Ibn Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said that day: "If I gain victory over the killer of Hamza, I will mutilate him in a manner that the Arabs will speak of." Hind and others with her had mutilated him, and so this verse was revealed.

The second: On the day of Uhud, sixty-four of the Ansar were struck, and six of the Muhajirun, among them Hamza, and they mutilated their dead. The Ansar said: "If we ever gain over them at some time, we will surely exceed their number twofold." So this verse was revealed. This was related by Ubayy ibn Ka'b.

(p-508) Abu Salih related from Ibn Abbas that the Muslims said: "If Allah enables us over them, we will mutilate the living, let alone the dead." So this verse was revealed, meaning: If you are going to do it, then mutilate the dead, as they mutilated your dead. Ibn al-Anbari said: He named the act of the polytheists "retaliation," though they had initiated the mutilation, in order that the two expressions would be paired and lighter on the tongue, as in His saying: ﴿And the recompense for an evil is an evil like it﴾ [al-Shura: 40].

**Section**

The scholars differed as to whether this [verse] is abrogated (mansukha, i.e., superseded by a later ruling) or not, on two views.

The first: It was revealed before (Bara'a), and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was commanded to fight whoever fought him, but not to initiate fighting. Then that was abrogated (naskh) and he was commanded to wage jihad. This was said by Ibn Abbas and al-Dahhak. On this view the meaning is: ﴿And if you are patient﴾ regarding fighting. Then this was abrogated by His saying: ﴿Kill the polytheists wherever you find them﴾ [al-Tawba: 5].

The second: It is muhkam (not abrogated, i.e., its ruling stands), and it was revealed only concerning one who has been wronged with an injustice; it is not lawful for him to take from his wrongdoer more than what the wrongdoer took from him. This was said by Mujahid, al-Sha'bi, al-Nakha'i, Ibn Sirin, and al-Thawri. On this view the meaning is: And if you are patient regarding mutilation, not regarding fighting.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿But be patient, and your patience is not except by Allah﴾, i.e., by His enabling and His help. This is a command to resolve (al-'azima, the firm course).

Regarding His saying: ﴿And do not grieve over them﴾ there are two views:

The first: over the disbelievers of Mecca, if they do not accept Islam. This was said by Abu Salih from Ibn Abbas.

The second: Do not grieve over the slain of Uhud, for they have gone to the mercy of Allah. This was mentioned by Ali ibn Ahmad al-Nisaburi.

(p-509) His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And do not be in distress﴾. Most readers recited ضَيْقٍ with a fatha on the ض. Ibn Kathir recited فِي ضِيقٍ with a kasra on the ض here and in (al-Naml: 70).
